questions.answer: Substances with all electrons paired and weakly repelled by magnetic field.

questions.text: Give one property common to both hcp and ccp lattices.
questions.answer: Same coordination number (12).

questions.text: Write relation between radius of atom and edge length of fcc unit cell.
Draw diagram of bcc unit cell.
questions.answer: Diagram of bcc unit cell.

questions.text: Number of tetrahedral voids formed if number of atoms is N/2.
questions.answer: N

questions.text: Percentage of empty space in bcc lattice.
Calculate volume occupied by particles in simple cubic unit cell.
Number of octahedral voids in 0.5 mol of hcp structure.
Distinguish between crystalline and amorphous solids.
questions.answer: Crystalline solids have regular arrangement, sharp melting point, anisotropic nature; amorphous solids have random arrangement, no sharp melting point and are isotropic.

questions.text: Classify Pb, MgF2, SO2 and quartz.
questions.answer: Pb–metallic, MgF2–ionic, SO2–molecular, Quartz–covalent.

questions.text: Find number of atoms in fcc unit cell.
questions.answer: 4 atoms per unit cell.

questions.text: Explain vacancy defect with diagram.
questions.answer: Vacancy defect occurs when atoms are missing from lattice points, decreasing density.

questions.text: Calculate number of unit cells in 0.3 g of species.
Find unit cell edge length if diameter of atom is 120 pm in bcc.
Calculate packing efficiency for bcc lattice.
questions.answer: Packing efficiency of bcc lattice is 68%.

questions.text: Explain arrangement of spheres in hcp structure.
questions.answer: hcp structure has ABAB stacking of layers.

questions.text: Calculate molar mass of substance in fcc lattice.
questions.answer: 161.1 g mol⁻¹

questions.text: Find radius of sodium atom given density.
Classify nonstoichiometric point defects.
questions.answer: Metal deficiency and metal excess defects.

questions.text: Explain diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances.
questions.answer: Based on presence and alignment of unpaired electrons.

questions.text: What are nonstoichiometric point defects? Explain formation of F-centres.
questions.answer: Nonstoichiometric defects occur when ratio of ions differs from ideal. F-centres are electrons trapped in anion vacancies causing colour.

questions.text: Give classification of stoichiometric point defects and explain solid solutions.
questions.answer: Vacancy, interstitial, Schottky and Frenkel defects; solid solutions involve substitutional or interstitial atoms.

questions.text: Derive relation between density, molar mass and unit cell edge length.
questions.answer: ρ = nM / a³NA

questions.text: The coordination number of atoms in a body centred cubic (bcc) lattice is:
The number of atoms per unit cell in face centred cubic lattice is:
Which of the following solids is a non-stoichiometric compound?
questions.answer: ZnO

questions.text: Define unit cell.
questions.answer: A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the entire crystal.

questions.text: What is coordination number?
questions.answer: Coordination number is the number of nearest neighbouring particles surrounding a given particle in a crystal lattice.

questions.text: Define Schottky defect.
questions.answer: Schottky defect is a point defect in which equal number of cations and anions are missing from their lattice sites in an ionic crystal.

questions.text: Define Frenkel defect.
questions.answer: Frenkel defect is a point defect in which an ion leaves its lattice site and occupies an interstitial position.

questions.text: Distinguish between Schottky defect and Frenkel defect.
questions.answer: Schottky defect involves missing ions from lattice sites, while Frenkel defect involves displacement of an ion to interstitial site.

questions.text: Calculate the number of atoms per unit cell in a simple cubic lattice.
questions.answer: A simple cubic lattice has 8 corner atoms each contributing 1/8, so total atoms per unit cell = 1.

questions.text: Gold crystallises in a face centred cubic lattice. Calculate its density if the atomic mass is given and edge length of unit cell is known.
questions.answer: Density is calculated using ρ = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA). Substituting values gives density ≈ 19.3 g/cm³.

questions.text: An element crystallises in bcc structure. If the edge length of unit cell is given, calculate the atomic radius.
questions.answer: For bcc lattice, atomic radius r = (√3 × a) / 4.

questions.text: Explain different types of point defects found in ionic solids.
questions.answer: Point defects include Schottky defect, Frenkel defect and impurity defect affecting density and electrical properties.

questions.text: Ionic solids are hard and brittle.
questions.answer: Because shifting of layers brings like charges together causing strong repulsion and fracture.

questions.text: Frenkel defect does not affect density of a crystal.
questions.answer: Because ions are displaced within the lattice without changing total number of ions.

chapters.title: Solutions
chapters.description: Types of solutions, concentration terms, solubility, vapor pressure of solutions, Raoult's law, ideal and non-ideal solutions, colligative properties and abnormal molar mass.
topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van't Hoff Factor
learningObjectives: Classify solutions based on physical state and concentration.
Use different concentration units to express composition of solutions.
Explain Raoult's law and distinguish between ideal and non-ideal solutions.
Define and apply various colligative properties to determine molar mass.
Explain abnormal molar mass using van't Hoff factor.

questions.text: Which concentration term is temperature independent?
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: State Raoult's law for a solution of volatile liquids.
questions.answer: Raoult's law states that the partial vapour pressure of each component in an ideal solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

questions.text: Calculate the molality of a solution prepared by dissolving 18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) in 90 g of water.
questions.answer: Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol; mass of solvent = 0.090 kg; molality = 0.1 / 0.090 ≈ 1.11 m.

questions.text: Which of the following is a colligative property?
questions.answer: Relative lowering of vapour pressure

questions.text: Differentiate between ideal and non-ideal solutions on the basis of enthalpy change of mixing.
questions.answer: In ideal solutions, enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix) is zero, whereas in non-ideal solutions ΔHmix is not zero (it may be positive or negative).

questions.text: A solution containing 1.0 g of a non-volatile solute in 100 g of water boils at 100.15°C. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (Kb for water = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹).
questions.answer: ΔTb = 0.15 K; molality = ΔTb / Kb = 0.15 / 0.52 ≈ 0.288 m. Moles of solute = 0.288 × 0.100 = 0.0288 mol. Molar mass = 1.0 / 0.0288 ≈ 34.7 g mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Define solubility. How does temperature affect solubility of solids in liquids?
questions.answer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Generally, solubility of solids in liquids increases with increase in temperature.

questions.text: For a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law:
questions.answer: ΔHmix > 0 and ΔVmix > 0

questions.text: What is van't Hoff factor? How is it related to abnormal molar mass?
questions.answer: van't Hoff factor (i) is the ratio of the observed colligative property to the calculated colligative property for a nonelectrolyte. Due to association or dissociation, the effective number of particles changes, giving abnormal molar mass, which is corrected by using i.

questions.text: Explain the concept of azeotropes. Distinguish between minimum boiling and maximum boiling azeotropes with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Azeotropes are constant boiling mixtures whose composition in liquid and vapour phase is the same. Minimum boiling azeotropes show positive deviation and boil at a temperature lower than that of either component (e.g. ethanol–water). Maximum boiling azeotropes show negative deviation and boil at a temperature higher than either component (e.g. HNO₃–water).

questions.text: Sugar dissolves in water because
options: it forms hydrogen bonding with water
sugar and water are both polar
questions.answer: it forms hydrogen bonding with water

questions.text: The solubility of a gas in water
questions.answer: decreases with increase in temperature

questions.text: The units of Henry's law constant are
questions.answer: bar

questions.text: The colligative properties of solutions
options: depend on nature of solute particles
do not depend on number of solute particles
do not depend on association or dissociation of solute
depend on number of solute particles
questions.answer: depend on number of solute particles

questions.text: The solution which has maximum vapour pressure
questions.answer: pure solvent

questions.text: According to Raoult's law, relative lowering of vapour pressure of solution containing nonvolatile solute
options: is equal to mole fraction of solvent
is equal to mole fraction of solute
does not depend on mole fraction
is equal to molality of solution
questions.answer: is equal to mole fraction of solute

questions.text: Freezing point depression constant of a solvent is
questions.answer: independent of molality

questions.text: Which statement is applicable for 0.1 M urea solution and 0.1 M sucrose solution?
options: osmotic pressure of urea is greater
osmotic pressure of sucrose is greater
questions.answer: both have same osmotic pressure

questions.text: The Henry's law constant of a gas is 6.5 × 10⁴ bar. Its solubility in water is
questions.answer: 2.25 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹

questions.text: What are hypertonic solutions?
questions.answer: Solutions having higher osmotic pressure than another solution.

questions.text: What is cryoscopic constant?
questions.answer: It is the depression in freezing point produced by 1 molal solution.

questions.text: Write the effect of dissolution of nonvolatile solute on freezing point.
questions.answer: Freezing point of solvent is lowered.

questions.text: Write expression for relative lowering of vapour pressure.
questions.answer: ΔP / P° = x₂

questions.text: State Raoult's law.
questions.answer: Partial vapour pressure of a component is proportional to its mole fraction.

questions.text: State Henry's law.
questions.answer: Solubility of gas in liquid is directly proportional to pressure.

questions.text: Which type of solutions show positive deviation from Raoult's law?
questions.answer: Solutions with weaker solute–solvent interactions.

questions.text: What is enthalpy change and volume change of mixing of ideal solutions?
questions.answer: Both are zero.

questions.text: Define vapour pressure.
questions.answer: Pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with liquid.

questions.text: Write osmotic pressure equation for dilute solution.
questions.answer: π = CRT

questions.text: Distinguish between ideal and nonideal solutions.
questions.answer: Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law; nonideal solutions do not.

questions.text: Explain lowering of vapour pressure.
questions.answer: Nonvolatile solute reduces number of solvent molecules escaping into vapour.

questions.text: Differentiate between Kf and Kb.
questions.answer: Kf relates to freezing point depression, Kb to boiling point elevation.

questions.text: Which solution has higher freezing point depression: 0.05 M KCl or 0.05 M Al2(SO4)3?
Calculate elevation in boiling point when 30 g solute is dissolved.
Derive relation between molar mass and boiling point elevation.
Explain osmotic pressure using thistle funnel experiment.
questions.answer: Osmosis occurs through semipermeable membrane creating pressure difference.

questions.text: Explain phenomenon of osmosis.
questions.answer: Flow of solvent from dilute to concentrated solution through membrane.

questions.text: Explain elevation of boiling point.
questions.answer: Addition of solute lowers vapour pressure requiring higher temperature to boil.

questions.text: Calculate molar mass using osmotic pressure data.
questions.answer: 342 g mol⁻¹

questions.text: Calculate vapour pressure of solution.
Explain nonideal solutions with positive and negative deviations from Raoult's law.
questions.answer: Positive deviation occurs when solute–solvent interactions are weaker; negative when stronger.

questions.text: Explain lowering of freezing point using vapour pressure–temperature curves.
questions.answer: Freezing point of solution is lower due to reduced vapour pressure.

questions.text: Explain semipermeable membrane, osmosis and osmotic pressure.
questions.answer: Semipermeable membrane allows solvent flow creating osmotic pressure.

questions.text: The concentration of a solution expressed as number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent is called:
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: Which of the following is temperature independent?
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: Define molarity.
questions.answer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute present in one litre of solution.

questions.text: What is mole fraction?
questions.answer: Mole fraction is the ratio of number of moles of a component to total moles of all components in the solution.

questions.text: State Raoult's law.
questions.answer: Raoult's law states that the partial vapour pressure of a component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

questions.text: Define ideal solution.
questions.answer: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration and shows no enthalpy or volume change on mixing.

questions.text: What is azeotrope?
questions.answer: An azeotrope is a mixture of liquids that boils at a constant temperature and has same composition in liquid and vapour phase.

questions.text: Explain positive deviation from Raoult's law.
questions.answer: Positive deviation occurs when solute–solvent interactions are weaker than solute–solute or solvent–solvent interactions.

questions.text: Calculate molarity of a solution containing given grams of solute dissolved in given volume of solution.
questions.answer: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.

questions.text: Calculate mole fraction of each component in a binary solution.
questions.answer: Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles of solution.

questions.text: Calculate the elevation in boiling point of a solution given molal concentration and ebullioscopic constant.
questions.answer: ΔTb = Kb × m.

questions.text: Calculate depression in freezing point of a solution given molality and cryoscopic constant.
questions.answer: ΔTf = Kf × m.

questions.text: Explain non-ideal solutions with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Non-ideal solutions do not obey Raoult's law and show positive or negative deviation, e.g., ethanol–water mixture.

questions.text: Molality is preferred over molarity in colligative properties.
questions.answer: Because molality is temperature independent while molarity depends on volume which changes with temperature.

chapters.title: Ionic Equilibria
chapters.description: Concept of acids and bases, ionization of weak electrolytes, Ostwald's dilution law, pH scale, buffer solutions, solubility product and common ion effect.
topics: Arrhenius, Bronsted–Lowry and Lewis Acids and Bases
pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
learningObjectives: Compare different concepts of acids and bases.
Derive and apply Ostwald's dilution law for weak electrolytes.
Calculate pH of strong and weak acid/base solutions.
Explain the working of buffer solutions using Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
Use solubility product to predict precipitation and solubility.

questions.text: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?
questions.answer: BF₃

questions.text: State Ostwald's dilution law for a weak electrolyte.
questions.answer: Ostwald's dilution law states that the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte is inversely proportional to the square root of its concentration and relates dissociation constant K to concentration c and degree of dissociation α by K = cα² / (1 − α).

questions.text: Calculate the pH of 0.001 M HCl solution.
questions.answer: HCl is a strong acid and fully ionizes. [H⁺] = 0.001 M = 10⁻³ M; pH = −log[H⁺] = 3.

questions.text: The ionic product of water (Kw) at 25°C is approximately:
What is a buffer solution? Give one example each of acidic and basic buffer.
questions.answer: A buffer solution resists change in pH on addition of small amounts of acid or base. Example of acidic buffer: CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻Na⁺; basic buffer: NH₄OH and NH₄Cl.

questions.text: Write Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer and explain each term.
questions.answer: For an acidic buffer, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]), where pKa is −log Ka, [salt] is concentration of conjugate base and [acid] is concentration of weak acid.

questions.text: The solubility product of AgCl at 25°C is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. Calculate its solubility in mol L⁻¹ in pure water.
questions.answer: For AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = s²; s = √(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹.

questions.text: Common ion effect is observed when:
options: A weak electrolyte is mixed with a strong electrolyte having a common ion
A salt is added to a non-aqueous solvent
questions.answer: A weak electrolyte is mixed with a strong electrolyte having a common ion

questions.text: Explain hydrolysis of salts formed from (i) strong acid and weak base, (ii) weak acid and strong base with suitable examples.
questions.answer: i) Salts of strong acid and weak base (e.g. NH₄Cl) hydrolyse to give acidic solution because the cation reacts with water to produce H⁺. ii) Salts of weak acid and strong base (e.g. CH₃COONa) hydrolyse to give basic solution because the anion reacts with water to produce OH⁻.

questions.text: Derive the expression for pH of a weak acid solution using its dissociation constant (Ka) and concentration.
questions.answer: For weak acid HA of initial concentration C, degree of dissociation α is small. Ka = Cα²/(1−α) ≈ Cα². [H⁺] = Cα = √(CKa). Hence pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(√(C Ka)) = 1/2 (pKa − log C).

questions.text: What is the percentage dissociation of 0.1 M solution of acetic acid? [Ka(CH3COOH) = 10⁻⁵]
For the reaction HCl(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H3O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), which is a conjugate acid-base pair?
questions.answer: H3O⁺ and H2O

questions.text: In biochemical system, pH of blood is maintained due to which buffer?
questions.answer: HCO3⁻ + H2CO3

questions.text: If IP is ionic product and Ksp is solubility product, precipitation occurs when
questions.answer: IP > Ksp

questions.text: NH4F is a salt of weak acid HF and weak base NH4OH. The solution will be
questions.answer: slightly acidic

questions.text: The theory which explains amphoteric nature of water is
questions.answer: Bronsted–Lowry theory

questions.text: The pKb of weak base BOH [Kb = 1 × 10⁻⁵] is
Name the buffer used to maintain pH 8–10 for precipitation of IIIA group cations.
questions.answer: NH4OH + NH4Cl buffer

questions.text: Write the solubility product expression for Bi2S3.
questions.answer: Ksp = [Bi³⁺]²[S²⁻]³

questions.text: What is the pOH if hydrogen ion concentration is 1 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³?
Write the relation between molar solubility (S) and Ksp for CaF2.
questions.answer: Ksp = 4S³

questions.text: Give one example of salt derived from weak acid and weak base.
questions.answer: Ammonium acetate (CH3COONH4)

questions.text: Write the formula to calculate pH of acidic buffer solution.
questions.answer: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid])

questions.text: Calculate the pOH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl solution.
Calculate the pH and pOH of 0.0001 M HCl solution.
questions.answer: pH = 4, pOH = 10

questions.text: The solubility product of BaCl2 is 4.0 × 10⁻⁸. Find its molar solubility.
questions.answer: 2.154 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³

questions.text: Classify Cl⁻, NH4⁺, BCl3 and NH3 into Lewis acids and bases.
questions.answer: Cl⁻ and NH3 are Lewis bases; NH4⁺ and BCl3 are Lewis acids

questions.text: Define pH and pOH.
questions.answer: pH = −log[H⁺], pOH = −log[OH⁻]

questions.text: Define molar solubility and write its unit.
questions.answer: Moles dissolved per litre of saturated solution; unit mol L⁻¹

questions.text: Write solubility product expressions for BaSO4 and CaF2.
questions.answer: BaSO4: Ksp = [Ba²⁺][SO4²⁻]; CaF2: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]²

questions.text: Define buffer solution and explain its types.
questions.answer: Buffer solutions resist pH change; types are acidic and basic buffers.

questions.text: Write one application of citrate buffer, bicarbonate buffer and NH4OH + NH4Cl buffer.
questions.answer: Citrate buffer stabilizes penicillin; bicarbonate buffer maintains blood pH; NH4OH + NH4Cl used in qualitative analysis.

questions.text: Derive relation showing degree of dissociation of weak acid is inversely proportional to square root of concentration.
questions.answer: α = √(Ka / c)

questions.text: Calculate pOH of buffer containing NH4OH and NH4Cl.
Calculate Ksp of AgBr if its solubility is 1.20 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.
Derive the equation pH + pOH = 14 and distinguish between strong and weak electrolytes.
questions.answer: From Kw = 10⁻¹⁴, pH + pOH = 14; strong electrolytes dissociate completely, weak electrolytes partially.

questions.text: If S is solubility and Ksp is solubility product, derive relation for CaF2 and BaSO4. Calculate [H3O⁺] for pH 3.5.
questions.answer: CaF2: Ksp = 4S³; BaSO4: Ksp = S²; [H3O⁺] = 3.162 × 10⁻⁴ M

questions.text: Explain amphoteric nature of water. Define solubility product and hydrolysis of salt.
questions.answer: Water acts as acid and base; solubility product is ionic product at saturation; hydrolysis is reaction of salt with water.

questions.text: The pH of a neutral solution at 25°C is:
Which of the following is a weak acid?
questions.answer: CH₃COOH

questions.text: Define pH.
questions.answer: pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration of a solution.

questions.text: What is ionic product of water?
questions.answer: Ionic product of water is the product of concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxide ions in water.

questions.text: Define dissociation constant of an acid (Ka).
questions.answer: Ka is the equilibrium constant for dissociation of a weak acid into ions in aqueous solution.

questions.text: What is buffer solution?
questions.answer: A buffer solution resists change in pH on addition of small amount of acid or base.

questions.text: Give one example of acidic buffer.
questions.answer: Acetic acid and sodium acetate mixture is an acidic buffer.

questions.text: Calculate pH of a given concentration of strong acid.
questions.answer: pH = −log[H⁺], where [H⁺] equals concentration of strong acid.

questions.text: Calculate pH of a weak acid using Ka value.
questions.answer: pH is calculated using [H⁺] = √(Ka × C).

questions.text: Calculate pH of a buffer solution containing given concentration of weak acid and its salt.
questions.answer: pH is calculated using Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).

questions.text: Calculate solubility of a sparingly soluble salt using Ksp value.
questions.answer: Solubility is calculated using Ksp expression based on dissociation stoichiometry.

questions.text: Explain common ion effect with suitable example.
questions.answer: Common ion effect is suppression of ionisation of a weak electrolyte by addition of strong electrolyte having common ion.

questions.text: pH of pure water changes with temperature.
questions.answer: Because ionic product of water varies with temperature.

questions.text: Buffer solutions are important in biological systems.
questions.answer: Because they maintain nearly constant pH essential for biochemical reactions.

chapters.title: Chemical Thermodynamics
chapters.description: Basic thermodynamic terms, first law, enthalpy changes, Hess's law, spontaneity, entropy, Gibbs free energy and criteria for equilibrium.
topics: System, Surroundings and Types of Systems
Heat of Reaction and Hess's Law
Gibbs Free Energy and Work Function
Relationship between ΔG, ΔH and ΔS
learningObjectives: Define system, surroundings and types of thermodynamic systems.
Apply first law of thermodynamics to physical and chemical processes.
Explain enthalpy changes and use Hess's law for calculation.
Describe entropy and spontaneity in terms of second law.
Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to predict feasibility of reactions.

questions.text: Which of the following is an extensive property?
questions.answer: Enthalpy

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. Mathematically, ΔU = q + w.

questions.text: An ideal gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Calculate the change in internal energy of the system.
State Hess's law of constant heat summation.
questions.answer: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in a series of steps.

questions.text: For a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure:
questions.answer: ΔG < 0

questions.text: Define entropy. What is its SI unit?
questions.answer: Entropy is a measure of randomness or disorder of a system. Its SI unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Calculate ΔG for a reaction at 298 K if ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Comment on spontaneity.
questions.answer: Convert ΔS to kJ: −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = −0.050 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −40 − 298(−0.050) = −40 + 14.9 = −25.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Since ΔG < 0, the reaction is spontaneous.

questions.text: Which of the following processes has ΔS > 0?
options: Dissolution of a salt in water
Formation of ionic solid from gaseous ions
questions.answer: Dissolution of a salt in water

questions.text: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Reversible processes occur infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states and can be reversed by an infinitesimal change (e.g. isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas). Irreversible processes occur spontaneously in a finite time with driving force; they cannot be exactly reversed (e.g. free expansion of gas, natural heat flow from hot to cold body).

questions.text: Explain the relationship ΔG = −nFE and its significance in electrochemical cells.
questions.answer: ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work obtainable from a galvanic cell. For a cell involving n moles of electrons and emf E, ΔG = −nFE (F is Faraday constant). A negative ΔG corresponds to positive E and a spontaneous cell reaction.

questions.text: An intensive property among the following is
questions.answer: temperature

questions.text: The value of 1 dm³ bar is
The work done in the dm³ bar when 200 mL of ethylene gas and 150 mL of HCl gas react at 1 bar pressure is
The work done in vacuum when 300 mmol of an ideal gas expands until its volume is increased by 2.3 dm³ at 1 bar pressure is
questions.answer: zero

questions.text: For an isothermal process
questions.answer: ΔU = 0

questions.text: For an isochoric process
questions.answer: ΔV = 0

questions.text: The change in internal energy when 2 kJ of heat is released by the system and 6 kJ of work is done on the system is
questions.answer: +4 kJ

questions.text: Write the expression for maximum work done when 1 mole of ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly.
questions.answer: Wmax = 2.303 RT log(V2/V1)

questions.text: Write the mathematical relation between ΔH and ΔU for formation of one mole of CO2 under standard conditions.
questions.answer: ΔH = ΔU

questions.text: Standard enthalpy change for formation of water is −286 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate enthalpy change for formation of 0.018 kg of water.
Write the expression of first law of thermodynamics for an isothermal process.
questions.answer: W = Q

questions.text: What is the sign convention when work is done on the system?
questions.answer: Work done on the system is positive

questions.text: Write the relation between enthalpy change and internal energy change for gaseous reaction.
questions.answer: ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT

questions.text: Define standard enthalpy of combustion and enthalpy of sublimation.
questions.answer: Standard enthalpy of combustion is enthalpy change when one mole of substance is completely burnt; enthalpy of sublimation is enthalpy change when solid converts directly into vapour.

questions.text: State and explain Hess's law of constant heat summation.
questions.answer: Total enthalpy change of reaction is independent of the path and equals sum of enthalpy changes of individual steps.

questions.text: Write the features of reversible process.
questions.answer: Occurs infinitesimally slowly, system remains in equilibrium, reversible by small change.

questions.text: Derive expression for pressure–volume work.
questions.answer: W = −Pext (V2 − V1)

questions.text: Calculate C–Cl bond enthalpy from given data.
questions.answer: 330 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.text: Calculate standard enthalpy of combustion of methane.
questions.answer: −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define isolated system and calculate work done when gas expands isothermally.
questions.answer: Isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter; work done = −600 J

questions.text: Define enthalpy of fusion and derive expression for maximum work.
questions.answer: Enthalpy change when solid melts; Wmax = 2.303 nRT log(V2/V1)

questions.text: Derive expression for work done in chemical reaction and relation between ΔH and ΔU for isochoric process.
questions.answer: W = −ΔngRT; ΔH = ΔU

questions.text: Define standard enthalpy of formation with example.
questions.answer: Enthalpy change when one mole of compound forms from elements in standard state.

questions.text: Calculate final pressure when CO2 is compressed isothermally and reversibly.
Define enthalpy of atomization and extensive properties. Calculate standard enthalpy of formation of methanol.
questions.answer: Enthalpy of atomization is enthalpy change for formation of gaseous atoms; extensive properties depend on amount of matter; ΔHf° of CH3OH = −239 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define bond enthalpy and enthalpy of ionisation. Calculate standard enthalpy of reaction.
questions.answer: Bond enthalpy is energy to break bond; enthalpy of ionisation is energy to remove electron; ΔH° = −822.4 kJ

questions.text: Calculate heat evolved when CO reacts with NO2 and explain thermochemical equation.
questions.answer: Heat evolved = 128.58 kJ; thermochemical equation includes enthalpy change.

questions.text: Classify properties into intensive and extensive. Define state function with examples.
questions.answer: Pressure and temperature are intensive; mass and volume are extensive; state function depends only on state.

questions.text: Which of the following is a state function?
questions.answer: Internal energy

questions.text: The SI unit of enthalpy change is:
questions.answer: J mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define system in thermodynamics.
questions.answer: A system is that part of the universe which is under observation.

questions.text: What is enthalpy?
questions.answer: Enthalpy is the total heat content of a system and is represented by H.

questions.text: State first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed but can be converted from one form to another.

questions.text: Define internal energy.
questions.answer: Internal energy is the total energy possessed by a system due to molecular motion and interactions.

questions.text: What is Hess's law of constant heat summation?
questions.answer: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the path and depends only on initial and final states.

questions.text: Calculate work done when a gas expands against constant external pressure.
questions.answer: Work done is calculated using w = −PΔV.

questions.text: Calculate change in internal energy using first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: ΔU = q + w.

questions.text: Calculate enthalpy change of a reaction using given thermochemical equations.
questions.answer: Enthalpy change is calculated using Hess's law by algebraic addition of equations.

questions.text: Calculate standard enthalpy of formation using given data.
questions.answer: Standard enthalpy of formation is calculated from thermochemical equations under standard conditions.

questions.text: Explain types of thermodynamic systems.
questions.answer: Thermodynamic systems are classified as open, closed and isolated systems.

questions.text: Enthalpy is a state function.
questions.answer: Because it depends only on initial and final states of the system, not on the path.

questions.text: Heat is not a state function.
questions.answer: Because heat depends on the path followed during a process.

chapters.title: Electrochemistry

learningObjectives: Differentiate between electrolytic and galvanic cells.
Explain electrode potential and its measurement.
Apply Nernst equation to calculate cell potential.
Use electrochemical series to predict feasibility and EMF.
Describe working of important electrochemical cells and corrosion.

questions.text: Unit of molar conductance is:
questions.answer: S cm² mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define standard electrode potential.
questions.answer: Standard electrode potential is the potential difference between a metal/metal ion electrode and standard hydrogen electrode when the ionic concentration is 1 M, gas pressure 1 bar and temperature 298 K.

questions.text: Calculate the EMF of a cell: Zn | Zn²⁺ (0.1 M) || Cu²⁺ (1.0 M) | Cu. Given E°cell = 1.10 V, n = 2.
In an electrolytic cell, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is called:
questions.answer: Anode

questions.text: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
questions.answer: Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution, the limiting molar conductance of an electrolyte is equal to the sum of the individual contributions of its cation and anion.

questions.text: The limiting molar conductance of NaCl, HCl and NaAc are 126.4, 426.2 and 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹ respectively. Calculate the limiting molar conductance of CH₃COOH.
questions.answer: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(NaAc) − Λ°(NaCl) = 426.2 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.8 S cm² mol⁻¹.

questions.text: What is a fuel cell? Give one example.
questions.answer: A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel directly into electrical energy by an electrochemical reaction. Example: Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

questions.text: Rusting of iron is an example of:
questions.answer: Galvanic corrosion

questions.text: Explain the construction and working of a lead storage battery.
questions.answer: A lead storage battery consists of lead anode and lead dioxide cathode dipped in aqueous H₂SO₄. During discharge, Pb is oxidized to PbSO₄ and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄, producing electrical energy. On charging, these reactions are reversed, regenerating Pb and PbO₂.

questions.text: What is electrochemical series? Give any three applications.
questions.answer: Electrochemical series is an arrangement of elements in order of their standard reduction potentials. Applications: predicting feasibility of redox reactions, calculating EMF of cells, determining the oxidizing/reducing strength of species and metal displacement reactions.

questions.text: Kohlrausch law is applicable for the solution
options: concentrated as well as dilute solution
questions.answer: a saturated solution

questions.text: During electrolysis of molten NaCl, which statement is correct?
options: Na is liberated at cathode and Cl2 at anode
questions.answer: Na is liberated at cathode and Cl2 at anode

questions.text: The SI unit of conductivity is
questions.answer: S m⁻¹

questions.text: A graph between molar conductivity and √c is
options: a straight line passing through origin
a straight line not passing through origin
questions.answer: a straight line

questions.answer: Electrolytic cell uses electricity; galvanic cell produces electricity

questions.answer: An electrochemical cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy by redox reactions.

questions.text: Define standard electrode potential.
questions.answer: Standard electrode potential is electrode potential measured under standard conditions with respect to standard hydrogen electrode.

questions.text: State Nernst equation.
questions.answer: Nernst equation relates electrode potential to standard electrode potential and concentration of ions.

questions.text: What is salt bridge? State its function.
questions.answer: Salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality and completes the circuit by allowing ion flow.

questions.text: Calculate cell EMF using given standard electrode potentials.

questions.text: Calculate electrode potential at given concentration using Nernst equation.

questions.text: Calculate equilibrium constant of a cell reaction using EMF data.
questions.answer: Equilibrium constant is calculated using ΔG° = −nFE°cell and relation with K.

questions.text: Calculate electrical conductivity of solution given resistance and cell constant.
questions.answer: Conductivity κ = cell constant / resistance.

questions.text: Explain electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride.
questions.answer: Electrolysis produces hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode and sodium hydroxide in solution.

questions.text: Salt bridge is essential in galvanic cell.
questions.answer: Because it prevents charge build-up and maintains electrical neutrality.

questions.text: Conductivity of electrolyte decreases on dilution.
questions.answer: Because number of ions per unit volume decreases on dilution.

chapters.title: Chemical Kinetics
chapters.description: Rate of reaction, factors affecting rate, rate laws, order and molecularity, integrated rate equations, half-life, collision theory and catalysis.
topics: Average and Instantaneous Rate of Reaction
Integrated Rate Equations for Zero and First Order
learningObjectives: Define rate of reaction and express it mathematically.
Determine order and rate constant from experimental data.
Use integrated rate equations for zero and first order reactions.
Explain effect of temperature on rate using Arrhenius equation.
Describe collision theory and role of catalyst.

questions.text: The unit of rate constant for a first-order reaction is:
questions.answer: s⁻¹

questions.text: Define order of a reaction. How is it different from molecularity?
questions.answer: Order is the sum of powers of concentration terms in the rate law and is an experimental quantity. Molecularity is the number of molecules colliding in a single step and is a theoretical concept defined only for elementary reactions.

questions.text: For a first order reaction, the rate constant is 0.693 min⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.
questions.answer: For first order, t½ = 0.693 / k = 0.693 / 0.693 = 1 min.

questions.text: According to Arrhenius equation, rate constant k is related to temperature T as:
questions.answer: k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT)

questions.text: What is activation energy? How does a catalyst affect it?
questions.answer: Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reacting molecules must possess to undergo a chemical reaction. A catalyst lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway.

questions.text: A zero order reaction has a rate constant of 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. How long will it take for the concentration of reactant to fall from 0.10 mol L⁻¹ to 0.04 mol L⁻¹?
Write integrated rate law for first order reaction and explain the terms.
questions.answer: For A → products, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 − kt or [A]t = [A]0 e^(−kt); [A]0 is initial concentration, [A]t is concentration at time t, k is rate constant.

questions.text: Which factor does NOT affect rate of a chemical reaction?
questions.answer: Avogadro number

questions.text: Explain collision theory of bimolecular reactions.
questions.answer: According to collision theory, molecules must collide with sufficient energy (≥ activation energy) and proper orientation to react. Rate is proportional to the number of effective collisions per unit time. Temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing rate.

questions.text: Discuss the effect of temperature on rate constant using Arrhenius equation and explain how activation energy can be determined graphically.
questions.answer: Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) shows that k increases with temperature. Taking log gives ln k = ln A − Eₐ/RT. A plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R from which activation energy Eₐ is calculated.

questions.text: A first order reaction is 50% complete in 69.3 minutes. Time required for 90% completion is
Time required for 100% completion of zero order reaction is
questions.answer: a/k

questions.text: Rate constant of a reaction is 3.6 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. The order of reaction is
questions.answer: first

questions.text: The rate law relates the rate of a chemical reaction in terms of
questions.answer: concentration

questions.text: For first order reaction, the rate constant for decomposition of N2O5 is 6 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. The half-life period is
Order of reaction for which unit of rate constant is mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ is
The rate of catalysed reaction is larger than uncatalysed reaction as
questions.answer: Ea is lower

questions.text: Which of the following is unimolecular reaction?
questions.answer: PCl5 → PCl3 + Cl2

questions.text: Effect of catalyst in a chemical reaction is to change
questions.answer: activation energy

questions.text: Give one example of pseudo first order reaction.
questions.answer: Hydrolysis of methyl acetate

questions.text: Write order of reaction: 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2.
questions.answer: Zero order

questions.text: Write molecularity of reaction: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2.
Rate constant for reaction 2N2O5 → 4NO2 + O2 is 4.98 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Find order.
questions.answer: First order

questions.text: Write unit of rate constant for first order reaction.
questions.answer: s⁻¹

questions.text: Write integrated rate law for zero order reaction.
questions.answer: [A] = [A]₀ − kt

questions.text: Name the slowest step that determines rate in complex reaction.
questions.answer: Rate determining step

questions.text: Write rate law for reaction: 2NO + 2H2 → N2 + 2H2O.
questions.answer: Rate = k[NO]²[H2]

questions.text: What is half-life of first order reaction if concentration decreases from 0.8 M to 0.2 M in 12 hours?
questions.answer: 6 hours

questions.text: Differentiate between order of reaction and molecularity.
questions.answer: Order is experimentally determined; molecularity is number of reacting species in elementary step.

questions.text: For reaction 2NOBr → 2NO + Br2, rate law is rate = k[NOBr]². Find k if rate is 6.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and [NOBr] = 2 × 10⁻³ M.
questions.answer: 1.625 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

questions.text: Write two points about order of reaction.
questions.answer: Order can be zero or fractional; higher order reactions are rare.

questions.text: Explain pseudo first order reaction with example.
questions.answer: Reaction appears first order due to excess of one reactant, e.g., hydrolysis of ester.

questions.text: Define order of reaction.
questions.answer: Sum of powers of concentration terms in rate law.

questions.text: Explain catalysis with the help of potential energy diagram.
questions.answer: Catalyst lowers activation energy by providing alternate pathway.

questions.text: Derive integrated rate law for first order reaction.
Define molecularity and calculate time required for 80% decomposition of first order reaction.
questions.answer: Molecularity is number of reacting species; time = 1.16 min

questions.text: Write steps involved in reaction: NO2 + F2 → NO2F + F.
questions.answer: Slow step determines rate; intermediate F radical formed.

questions.text: Define rate law and write its units for zero and first order reactions.
questions.answer: Rate law relates rate to concentration; zero order: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, first order: s⁻¹

questions.text: For reaction 2A + B → C, if rate of disappearance of A is 0.076 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, find rate of formation of C.
questions.answer: 0.038 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

questions.text: In first order reaction A → B, 60% decomposes in 45 minutes. Find half-life and write rate law.
questions.answer: Half-life = 34 min; rate law = k[A]

questions.text: Derive relation between half-life and rate constant for first order reaction.
Give one example where order and molecularity are same. Explain factors affecting rate of reaction.
questions.answer: Example: 2NO2 → 2NO + O2; factors include concentration, temperature, catalyst.

questions.text: The rate of a chemical reaction is defined as:
options: Change in concentration per unit time
Change in temperature per unit time
Change in pressure per unit time
Change in volume per unit time
questions.answer: Change in concentration per unit time

questions.text: For a zero order reaction, the rate of reaction is:
questions.answer: Independent of concentration

questions.text: Define order of reaction.
questions.answer: Order of reaction is the sum of powers of concentration terms appearing in the rate law expression.

questions.text: What is rate constant?
questions.answer: Rate constant is the proportionality constant in the rate law equation at a given temperature.

questions.text: State integrated rate law for first order reaction.
questions.answer: For first order reaction: ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt.

questions.text: Define half-life of a reaction.
questions.answer: Half-life is the time required for the concentration of reactant to become half of its initial value.

questions.text: How does temperature affect the rate of reaction?
questions.answer: Increase in temperature increases kinetic energy of molecules, leading to higher reaction rate.

questions.text: Calculate rate constant for a first order reaction given concentration data and time.
questions.answer: Rate constant is calculated using integrated rate law: k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]).

questions.text: Calculate half-life of a first order reaction using given rate constant.
questions.answer: Half-life t½ = 0.693 / k.

questions.text: Calculate activation energy using Arrhenius equation given rate constants at two temperatures.
questions.answer: Activation energy is calculated using Arrhenius equation: ln(k₂/k₁) = Ea/R(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

questions.text: Calculate time required for a given percentage completion of first order reaction.
questions.answer: Time is calculated using integrated first order rate law.

questions.text: Explain collision theory of chemical reactions.
questions.answer: Collision theory states that effective collisions with sufficient energy and proper orientation lead to reaction.

questions.text: Half-life of a first order reaction is independent of initial concentration.
questions.answer: Because half-life depends only on rate constant, not on initial concentration.

questions.text: Rate constant increases with increase in temperature.
questions.answer: Because more molecules acquire activation energy at higher temperature.

chapters.title: Elements of Groups 16, 17 and 18
chapters.description: Study of p-block elements of groups 16, 17 and 18, their electronic configurations, trends, important compounds and anomalous behaviour of oxygen and fluorine.
topics: Group 16 Elements: O, S and Their Compounds
Hydrogen Halides and Oxyacids of Halogens
learningObjectives: Write electronic configurations of group 16, 17 and 18 elements.
Explain trends in physical and chemical properties down the groups.
Describe preparation and properties of important compounds like O₂, O₃, SO₂, H₂SO₄, Cl₂ and HCl.
Draw structures of oxyacids of sulphur and halogens.
Explain formation and structure of xenon compounds.

questions.text: Which of the following is a group 16 element?
questions.answer: Oxygen

questions.text: Why is O–O bond weaker than S–S bond?
questions.answer: Due to small size of oxygen atoms, electron–electron repulsions in O–O bond are higher, weakening the bond, whereas sulphur has larger size and less repulsion in S–S bond.

questions.text: Write any two uses of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Used in manufacture of fertilizers like ammonium sulphate and superphosphate; used in petroleum refining, dyes, paints and as a dehydrating agent.

questions.text: Which hydrogen halide is the strongest acid in aqueous solution?
questions.answer: HI

questions.text: What are interhalogen compounds? Give one example.
questions.answer: Compounds formed between different halogen atoms are called interhalogen compounds, e.g. ClF₃, ICl.

questions.text: Explain the structure and bonding in ozone (O₃).
questions.answer: Ozone is angular with O–O–O bond angle about 117°. It shows resonance between two equivalent structures with one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond, giving equalized bond order of 1.5.

questions.text: Why are noble gases chemically inert?
questions.answer: They have stable ns²np⁶ configuration (except He: 1s²) with completely filled valence shell and high ionization energy, so they do not easily gain or lose electrons.

questions.text: Which xenon compound has square planar geometry around xenon?
questions.answer: XeF₄

questions.text: Describe contact process for manufacture of sulphuric acid with reactions.
questions.answer: Steps: (i) Burning S or FeS₂ in air to form SO₂. (ii) Catalytic oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ using V₂O₅ at 720–770 K and 1–2 bar: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃. (iii) Absorption of SO₃ in conc. H₂SO₄ to form oleum, then dilution with water to get desired concentration of H₂SO₄.

questions.text: Explain anomalous behaviour of fluorine compared to other halogens.
questions.answer: Fluorine is most electronegative, smallest in size and has no d-orbitals. It forms only one oxidation state (−1), shows high reactivity, forms strong hydrogen bonds, low bond dissociation energy of F–F and does not form oxyacids like other halogens.

questions.text: Write balanced chemical reaction of sulfuric acid with carbon and sulfur.

questions.answer: Due to less stable electron configuration

Explain why fluorine shows only −1 oxidation state.

questions.answer: They differ in crystal shape, melting point and density

questions.text: Explain trend in atomic radius, electronegativity and electron gain enthalpy of group 16.
questions.answer: Radius increases, electronegativity decreases, electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative

questions.text: What are chalcogens? Explain preparation of SO2 from zinc sulfide.
questions.answer: Group 16 elements; SO2 prepared by roasting ZnS

questions.text: Explain manufacture of sulfuric acid by contact process.
questions.answer: Involves roasting, catalytic oxidation of SO2 and absorption to form H2SO4

questions.text: Explain reactions of chlorine with Al, Na, S8 and P4.
questions.answer: Forms AlCl3, NaCl, S2Cl2 and PCl3 respectively

questions.text: Draw structures of chloric acid and chlorous acid and explain anomalous behaviour of fluorine.
questions.answer: Fluorine shows anomalous behaviour due to small size and high electronegativity

questions.text: Which of the following is the most electronegative element among halogens?
questions.answer: Fluorine

questions.text: Which noble gas is used in electric bulbs?
questions.answer: Argon

questions.text: Name the element of group 16 having highest electronegativity.
questions.answer: Oxygen

questions.text: What are noble gases?
questions.answer: Noble gases are elements of group 18 having completely filled valence shells and low chemical reactivity.

questions.text: Give two uses of sulphur dioxide.
questions.answer: Sulphur dioxide is used as a bleaching agent and in manufacture of sulphuric acid.

questions.text: Explain anomalous behaviour of fluorine.
questions.answer: Fluorine shows anomalous behaviour due to its small size, high electronegativity and absence of d-orbitals.

questions.text: Why noble gases are chemically inert?
questions.answer: Because they have completely filled valence shells and high ionisation energies.

questions.text: Explain preparation, properties and uses of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Sulphuric acid is prepared by contact process; it is a strong acid and widely used in fertilizers, batteries and industries.

questions.text: Describe preparation and properties of chlorine.
questions.answer: Chlorine is prepared by electrolysis of brine; it is a greenish-yellow gas with strong oxidising properties.

questions.text: Explain preparation and uses of ozone.
questions.answer: Ozone is prepared by silent electric discharge and is used as an oxidising agent and disinfectant.

questions.text: Fluorine does not show positive oxidation state.
questions.answer: Because fluorine is the most electronegative element and cannot lose electrons.

questions.text: Helium is used in filling weather balloons.
questions.answer: Because helium is light, non-inflammable and inert.

learningObjectives: Write electronic configurations of transition and inner transition elements.
Explain general properties like variable oxidation state, catalytic activity and complex formation.
Interpret magnetic properties and colour on the basis of unpaired electrons.
Describe lanthanoid contraction and its consequences.
Differentiate between lanthanoids and actinoids.

questions.text: Which of the following is a d-block element?
questions.answer: Fe

questions.text: Why do transition metals show variable oxidation states?
questions.answer: Because of small energy difference between (n−1)d and ns orbitals, both can participate in bonding, giving multiple oxidation states.

questions.text: Explain why most transition metal salts are coloured.
questions.answer: Presence of partially filled d-orbitals allows d–d transitions of electrons under ligand field, absorbing certain wavelengths and giving colour.

questions.text: Which property generally increases with number of unpaired electrons?
questions.answer: Paramagnetism

questions.text: What is lanthanoid contraction?
questions.answer: It is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoids (from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺) with increasing atomic number due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.

questions.text: Give any three consequences of lanthanoid contraction.
questions.answer: i) Similarity in size of Zr and Hf and their similar properties. ii) Difficulty in separation of lanthanoids due to close radii. iii) Higher basicity of early lanthanoid hydroxides compared to later ones.

questions.text: Which of the following is an actinoid element?
questions.answer: Th

questions.text: Transition metals form alloys easily. Why?
questions.answer: Because their atomic sizes are similar and crystal structures are compatible, atoms of one metal can replace those of another in the lattice to form alloys.

questions.text: Compare lanthanoids and actinoids with respect to (i) oxidation states, (ii) radioactivity, (iii) complex formation.
questions.answer: i) Lanthanoids mainly show +3 state with few exceptions; actinoids show wider range from +3 to +6. ii) Most lanthanoids are non-radioactive (except promethium); almost all actinoids are radioactive. iii) Actinoids show stronger tendency for complex formation due to higher charge and larger size.

questions.text: An aqueous solution of a metal ion M²⁺ has three unpaired electrons. Calculate its magnetic moment (spin-only formula).

questions.answer: Fe3+

questions.text: Write chemical formula of zinc ore (zinc blende).
