questions.passageText: \[\begin{array}{c}\text{On the deck the Rover takes his stand,} \\ \text{So dark it is they see no land.} \\ \text{Quoth Sir Ralph, 'It will be lighter soon,} \\ \text{For there is the dawn of the rising Moon.'} \\ \\ \text{'Canst hear', said one, 'the breakers roar?} \\ \text{For methinks we should be near the shore.'} \\ \text{'Now, where we are I cannot tell,} \\ \text{But I wish we could hear the Inchcape Bell.'} \\ \\ \text{They hear no sound, the swell is strong,} \\ \text{Though the wind hath fallen they drift along;} \\ \text{Till the vessel strikes with a shivering shock,} \\ \text{'Oh Christ! It is the Inchcape Rock!'} \\ \\ \text{Sir Ralph the Rover tore his hair,} \\ \text{He curst himself in his despair;} \\ \text{The waves rush in on every side,} \\ \text{The ship is sinking beneath the tide.}\end{array} \]

subQuestions.text: Read the given extract and write a poetic appreciation of the poem with help of the following points.
options: About the poet and the title
Language/ poetic devices used in the poem
subQuestions.answer:
About the poet and the title: The poem 'The Rover' is written by Sir Walter Scott. It presents the emotional state of a sailor facing separation from his homeland.
Theme: The poem highlights patriotism, courage, adventure and the pain of separation from one's native land.
Poetic devices: The poet uses imagery, personification and alliteration to vividly describe the sea and the rover's emotions.
Special features: Dramatic setting, strong emotional appeal and simple narrative style enhance the poem.
Opinion: The poem effectively conveys the bravery and emotional strength of a sailor and evokes admiration for his sacrifice.

questions.question:
Appreciation : 
Read the extract and write the appreciation of the poem given below :
questions.passageText: \[ \begin{array}{c} \text{Is anybody happier because you passed his way?} \\ \text{Does anyone remember that you spoke to him today?} \\ \text{This day is almost over, and its toiling time is through;} \\ \text{Is there anyone to utter now a kindly word of you?} \\ \\ \text{Did you give a cheerful greeting to the friend who came along?} \\ \text{Or a churlish sort of 'Howdy' and then vanish in the throng?} \\ \text{Were you selfish pure and simple as you rushed along the way,} \\ \text{Or is someone mighty grateful for a deed you did today? } \\ \\ \text{Can you say tonight, in parting with the day that's slipping fast,} \\ \text{That you helped a single brother of the many that you passed?}\\ \text{Is a single heart rejoicing over what you did or said;} \\ \text{Does a man whose hopes were fading now with courage look ahead?} \\ \\ \text{Did you waste the day, or lose it, was it well or sorely spent?} \\ \text{Did you leave a trail of kindness or a scar of discontent?} \\ \text{As you close your eyes in slumber do you think that God would say,} \\ \text{You have earned one more tomorrow by the work you did today?} \end{array} \]

subQuestions.text: Read the given extract and write a poetic appreciation of the poem with help of the following points.
options: Form of the poem, theme and its significance
Poetic style, language features, poetic devices
Your opinion and critical evaluation of the poem.
subQuestions.answer:
About the poet and the title: The poem 'Have You Earned Your Tomorrow?' is written by Edgar Guest, popularly known as the people's poet for his simple and optimistic writing.
Theme: The poem emphasizes kindness, selfless service and moral responsibility towards others.
Poetic devices: The poem uses rhetorical questions, repetition and imagery to provoke self-reflection.
Special features: Simple language, direct questions and motivational tone make the poem impactful.
Opinion: The poem inspires readers to evaluate their daily actions and motivates them to lead a meaningful and compassionate life.

questions.question: Half yearly report of the student's council highlights the conduct of Braithwaite's class. Justify.
questions.answer: The half yearly report highlights the disciplined and responsible conduct of Braithwaite's class. The students showed maturity, cooperation and seriousness towards school activities. Their behaviour reflected respect for teachers and school rules, proving Braithwaite's positive influence on them.

questions.question: In the questioning session Denham was expressing few students' feelings. Illustrate.
questions.answer: During the questioning session, Denham voiced the doubts and concerns of many students. His questions reflected their curiosity, hesitation and desire to understand school decisions, making him a representative of the students' collective feelings.

questions.question: Miss Philips effectively handled the questioning session. Give supporting details.
questions.answer: Miss Philips handled the questioning session calmly and confidently. She answered students' questions patiently and logically, maintaining discipline and encouraging participation. Her composed attitude helped control the session and ensured a smooth interaction.

questions.question: Write a short note on the event which took place on 15th November in Greenslade School.
questions.answer: On 15th November, Greenslade School organised the presentation of the half yearly report of the students' council. Students presented their reports confidently on stage, highlighting class conduct, activities and achievements in front of teachers and fellow students.

questions.question: The extract presents the narrator as a silent observer of the events. Explain.
questions.answer: The narrator remains silent and observant throughout the extract. He carefully watches the students' presentations, questioning session and behaviour without interfering, allowing readers to understand the events objectively through his observations.

questions.question: 'Analyzing the change in the students' behaviour in the presentation' is the central theme. Explain.
questions.answer: The extract focuses on the transformation in students' behaviour. Initially nervous, they gradually gain confidence while presenting. This change highlights their growth, discipline and ability to take responsibility during the presentation.

questions.question: Denham and Miss Joseph played a key role in the presentation of the half yearly report of students' council. Illustrate.
questions.answer: Denham actively participated by raising questions that reflected students' thoughts, while Miss Joseph guided and supported the proceedings. Together, they ensured effective communication between students and teachers during the presentation.

questions.question: The senior students presented their class report more confidently than the junior students. Give reasons.
questions.answer: Senior students were more confident due to experience, maturity and familiarity with stage presentations. Juniors lacked confidence as they were new and less experienced, making seniors appear more composed and assured.

questions.question: Fernman was innovative and dramatic in his presentation. Discuss in brief.
questions.answer: Fernman used dramatic expressions, clear voice and confident body language in his presentation. His innovative style made the report engaging and impressive, capturing the attention of both teachers and students.

questions.question: The stage has a great impact on the presentations of the students. Justify the statement.
questions.answer: The stage influences students' confidence and performance. Some students feel nervous initially, while others gain confidence. Standing on stage encourages responsibility, seriousness and effective communication during presentations.

questions.question: Explain how the author has made use of International Date Line and time zones in his novel.
questions.answer: The author cleverly uses the International Date Line and time zones to create suspense. While travelling eastward, Phileas Fogg unknowingly gains a day. This scientific detail becomes crucial at the end, helping Fogg win the wager and proving the accuracy of modern geographical knowledge.

questions.question: 'Money was never a concern for Mr. Phileas Fogg; it was for honour he accepted the wager.' Discuss.
questions.answer: Mr. Phileas Fogg was a wealthy man and money held little importance for him. He accepted the wager to prove his punctuality, discipline and integrity. For him, winning meant maintaining honour and reputation rather than gaining financial benefit.

questions.question: Phileas Fogg's travel around the world was full of adventures and surprises. Illustrate.
questions.answer: Fogg's journey involved missed trains, storms at sea, arrests, rescues and cultural challenges. He saves Aouda, faces false accusations by Fix and overcomes delays with determination. These unexpected events make his world tour adventurous and thrilling.

questions.question: Explain how the time gained of a full day is revealed to Mr. Fogg.
questions.answer: Mr. Fogg believes he has lost the wager by a day. However, Passepartout realises they gained a day while travelling eastward across time zones. This revelation allows Fogg to reach the Reform Club on time and win the wager.

questions.question: Passepartout stations himself outside Phileas' door. Give reasons.
questions.answer: Passepartout waits outside Fogg's room because he feels guilty for the delays caused during the journey. He fears facing his master and anxiously hopes for forgiveness, showing his loyalty, concern and emotional attachment towards Mr. Fogg.

questions.question: Passepartout blamed himself for the misfortune of his master. Justify.
questions.answer: Passepartout considers himself responsible for the delays caused by Fix and other incidents. He believes his actions prevented Fogg from winning the wager. His self-blame highlights his honesty, loyalty and deep sense of responsibility towards his master.

questions.question: Compare the remorse in the minds of Mr. Fogg and Aouda for the seeming failure of his wager.
questions.answer: Mr. Fogg feels calm yet disappointed, accepting failure with dignity. Aouda, however, feels deeply guilty, believing she caused delays. While Fogg remains composed, Aouda's remorse is emotional, reflecting her gratitude and concern for him.

questions.question: Explain the stress on the mind of Fogg after returning from world tour at Saville Row.
questions.answer: After returning to Saville Row, Fogg believes he has lost the wager. He becomes quiet and withdrawn, mentally burdened by failure. Despite his inner stress, he maintains self-control and accepts the situation without complaint.

questions.question: Narrate the happenings at Reform Club on the 80th day of the wager.
questions.answer: Members of the Reform Club gather expecting Fogg's defeat. At the last moment, Fogg arrives exactly on time, proving his success. His punctual entry shocks everyone and confirms his victory in the wager.

questions.question: There was no general agreement about Mr. Fogg's success among the opponents. Discuss.
questions.answer: Many club members doubted Fogg's success due to delays, arrests and unexpected obstacles. Some believed modern transport made it possible, while others remained sceptical. This lack of agreement added tension and suspense to the wager.

questions.question: Narrate the happenings at a prison where Fogg was kept under arrest.
questions.answer: Mr. Fogg was wrongly arrested by Detective Fix on suspicion of bank robbery. He remained calm and dignified in prison. Later, Fix realised his mistake and Fogg was released, but the delay almost cost him the wager.

questions.question: 'All is well that ends well.' Justify in the light of the extract from the novel 'Around the World in Eighty Days.'
questions.answer: Despite numerous hardships, delays and apparent failure, Fogg ultimately wins the wager and gains Aouda's love. The successful conclusion proves that patience and perseverance lead to positive outcomes, justifying the statement 'All is well that ends well.'

questions.question: Winning the heart is preferred to the winning of wager. Express by supporting the details.
questions.answer: Though Fogg wins the wager, his greatest achievement is winning Aouda's love. Marriage brings him emotional fulfilment, proving that human relationships and compassion are more valuable than money or success in a wager.

questions.question: The reception of six pearls helps the story to move forward by providing some connection with the other happenings. Illustrate.
questions.answer: The six pearls connect Miss Morstan to her father's mysterious disappearance. They indicate the existence of a hidden treasure and unknown benefactors. This clue deepens the mystery and leads Holmes to investigate further, thereby moving the story forward.

questions.question: Describe the desired destination of the parties in your words by providing some details.
questions.answer: The parties aim to reach the third pillar near the Lyceum Theatre. It is a secret meeting place mentioned in the anonymous letter. This destination adds suspense as it is unfamiliar and linked to danger and mystery.

questions.question: Write the character sketch of Sherlock Holmes as a professional detective.
questions.answer: Sherlock Holmes is intelligent, observant and logical. He uses scientific reasoning and deep knowledge to solve cases. His keen observation, analytical thinking and confidence make him an exceptional professional detective.

questions.question: Compare the thought process of Holmes and Dr. Watson in handling the case.
questions.answer: Holmes relies on logic, observation and deduction, while Dr. Watson depends on emotions and assumptions. Holmes analyses facts scientifically, whereas Watson views situations from a human and sympathetic perspective.

questions.question: Narrate the case of Miss Morstan in your words.
questions.answer: Miss Morstan's father disappeared mysteriously, and she later began receiving pearls from an unknown sender. She seeks Holmes' help to uncover the truth behind her father's disappearance and the mysterious gifts.

questions.question: Sherlock Holmes deduced facts from the back files of the Times. Justify by providing few details.
questions.answer: Holmes examines old newspaper records to gather information about Captain Morstan. These records help him understand past events and connect them to the present mystery, showing his methodical approach.

questions.question: 'You are a wronged woman, and shall have justice'. Interpret the statement to highlight the conflict in Miss Morstan's mind.
questions.answer: Miss Morstan is torn between fear and hope. She desires justice for her father but fears the truth. Holmes' assurance reflects her inner conflict and her dependence on his intelligence.

questions.question: Dr. Watson reflects Miss Morstan's state of mind. Discuss with some examples.
questions.answer: Watson observes Miss Morstan's nervousness, fear and curiosity. His sympathetic narration mirrors her emotional state, helping readers understand her anxiety and vulnerability during the investigation.

questions.question: Holmes had a competence about the route of their travel. Suggest some points to clarify the statement.
questions.answer: Holmes plans the route carefully, choosing safe and strategic paths. His knowledge of London streets ensures timely arrival and protection, showing his foresight and preparedness.

questions.question: The mention of new places adds a pace to the story. Justify.
questions.answer: New locations introduce suspense and movement in the plot. Each place brings fresh clues and challenges, accelerating the story and maintaining the reader's interest.

questions.question: Miss Morstan found Holmes as the right person to handle her case. Give reason.
questions.answer: Miss Morstan trusts Holmes due to his reputation, intelligence and confidence. His logical approach and assurance convince her that he can uncover the truth behind her mysterious case.

questions.question: Write the character sketch of Dr. Watson as a sensitive character.
questions.answer: Dr. Watson is compassionate, caring and emotionally sensitive. He shows concern for Miss Morstan's comfort and feelings, making him a humane contrast to Holmes' logical personality.

questions.question: The paper found in the desk of Captain Morstan is the center of the action. Explain.
questions.answer: The paper reveals secret information about the treasure and meetings. It connects past and present events, driving the investigation and forming the core of the plot.

questions.question: “I may be very obtuse, Holmes, but I fail to see what this suggests.” Justify the statement by highlighting the difference in deducing the case.
questions.answer: Watson admits his inability to deduce facts like Holmes. This highlights Holmes' superior analytical skills and Watson's dependence on straightforward reasoning rather than deep deduction.

questions.question: Find support from the text which elaborates the tone of the narrator when he compares himself with Miss Morstan.
questions.answer: The narrator shows humility and sensitivity while comparing himself with Miss Morstan. His tone reflects admiration and concern, emphasizing her grace and emotional strength.

questions.question: The narrator makes Miss Morstan's journey comfortable while going to an unknown place. Narrate in your words.
questions.answer: Watson ensures Miss Morstan's comfort by offering reassurance and polite companionship. His protective attitude reduces her fear while travelling to an unfamiliar and possibly dangerous destination.

questions.question: 'The coachman is described as a faithful servant'. Justify the statement in your words.
questions.answer: The coachman follows instructions sincerely and shows loyalty to his employer. His obedience and reliability justify his description as a faithful servant.

questions.question: Holmes, Dr. Watson and Mary Morstan reached at the third pillar of the Lyceum Theatre. Describe the state of mind of the trio.
questions.answer: Holmes is alert and focused, Watson is cautious yet curious, and Miss Morstan is anxious but hopeful. Their mixed emotions reflect suspense and anticipation at this crucial stage of the investigation.

chapters.title: Population: Part 1
chapters.description: Concept of population distribution, density of population, physical and human factors affecting distribution, and an introduction to population growth.
topics: Human and economic factors affecting population distribution
learningObjectives: Define population distribution and population density.
Identify regions of high and low population density in the world.
Explain how relief, climate, soil and water affect population distribution.
Explain how agriculture, mining, transport, urbanisation and government policies affect population distribution.
Relate population growth with birth rate and death rate in a basic way.

questions.text: Population density is defined as:
options: Total population divided by total area
Total area divided by total population
Total population multiplied by total area
questions.answer: Total population divided by total area

questions.text: Name any two regions of the world which are sparsely populated and state one common reason.
questions.answer: Examples: Sahara desert and Arctic region. Common reason: extreme climatic conditions make human life difficult.

questions.text: Explain how relief (landforms) influence population distribution.
questions.answer: Flat and low-lying plains favour agriculture, transport and settlement, so they have high population density, whereas mountains and steep slopes hinder agriculture and transport, so they have low population density.

questions.text: Which of the following regions generally has the highest population density?
questions.answer: River valleys and deltas

questions.text: State any two human (non-physical) factors responsible for high population density.
questions.answer: Examples: developed transportation network, industrialisation, availability of employment opportunities, urbanisation.

questions.text: A country has a population of 50 million and an area of 250,000 sq km. Calculate its population density.
questions.answer: Density = 50,000,000 ÷ 250,000 = 200 persons per sq km.

questions.text: Explain with suitable examples how climate affects population distribution in the world.
questions.answer: Equable climates (e.g., Western Europe) attract dense population as agriculture and living conditions are favourable. Extreme hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian desert) and cold regions (Greenland, Antarctica) are sparsely populated due to lack of water, difficult agriculture and harsh living conditions. Very humid equatorial regions like Amazon basin also remain sparsely populated due to dense forests and diseases.

questions.text: What is meant by distribution of population?
questions.answer: Distribution of population refers to the way people are spread or arranged over the Earth's surface.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a physical factor affecting population distribution?
questions.answer: Government policy

questions.text: Distinguish between areas of high population density and areas of low population density on any three points.
questions.answer: Areas of high density: usually plains/coasts, fertile soils, developed transport, intensive agriculture/industry and urbanisation. Areas of low density: mountains/deserts/polar regions, infertile or thin soils, poor accessibility, limited economic activities and smaller/nucleated settlements.

questions.text: Broad base in population pyramid indicates higher number of children.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.answer: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.text: Arrange according to increase in age.
questions.answer: Children → Young people → Adults → Old people

questions.text: Population distribution is uneven.
questions.answer: Population distribution depends on physical, economic and social factors like climate, relief, soil, industries and transport.

questions.text: Distinguish between birth rate and death rate.
questions.answer: Birth rate refers to number of live births per thousand population per year, while death rate refers to number of deaths per thousand population per year.

questions.text: Explain uneven distribution of population with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Population is dense in fertile plains and industrial regions while sparse in deserts, mountains and polar regions.

questions.text: Show a country in second phase of demographic transition on the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Save map question image under /public/maps with standardized filename and reference it using imageUrl.
questions.answer: Example: Nigeria / India (as per map)

questions.text: Draw pyramid of underdeveloped countries.
questions.howToSaveImage: Scan diagram from answer key or textbook and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Broad base and narrow apex showing high birth rate.

questions.text: Explain the physical factors affecting the distribution of population.
questions.answer: Physical factors include climate, relief, soil, water availability and natural vegetation which influence settlement and population density.

chapters.title: Population: Part 2
chapters.description: Population composition including age structure, sex ratio, literacy, occupational structure, rural–urban composition, demographic dividend and migration.
learningObjectives: Interpret different types of population pyramids.
Explain age structure and dependency ratio.
Define sex ratio and discuss its spatial variation.
Explain the idea of demographic dividend with reference to India.
Classify types of migration and identify push and pull factors.

questions.text: Sex ratio in India is expressed as:
questions.answer: Number of females per 1000 males

questions.text: What is meant by age structure of population?
questions.answer: Age structure refers to the distribution of population in different age groups such as children, working-age people and the aged in a given region.

questions.text: Differentiate between expansive and constrictive population pyramids in brief.
questions.answer: Expansive pyramid has a broad base and narrow top, showing high birth and death rates and large child population. Constrictive pyramid has a narrow base and relatively wider upper part, showing low birth rate and larger proportion of older people.

questions.text: A country with very low birth and death rates and almost equal percentage in all age groups will show which type of pyramid?
questions.answer: Stationary

questions.text: Define demographic dividend.
questions.answer: Demographic dividend is the potential economic benefit that arises from a change in a country's age structure, when the share of working-age population becomes larger than the dependent population.

questions.text: Explain any three conditions necessary for a country like India to effectively utilise its demographic dividend.
questions.answer: Conditions: (1) Investment in quality education and skill development so that working-age people are employable. (2) Adequate job opportunities through industrial and service sector growth. (3) Good health facilities to keep workforce productive. (4) Gender equality and higher participation of women in labour force. (Any three explained.)

questions.text: Which of the following is a pull factor of migration?
options: Higher wages and better jobs in destination
questions.answer: Higher wages and better jobs in destination

questions.text: What is internal migration? Give one example.
questions.answer: Migration within the boundaries of the same country is called internal migration, e.g., a person moving from rural Odisha to Mumbai for work.

questions.text: Describe the effects of migration on the donor region and the recipient region (any three effects each).
questions.answer: Donor region: (i) Loss of working-age population can reduce production. (ii) Remittances sent by migrants can improve family income. (iii) Change in sex ratio and age structure as many young males move out. Recipient region: (i) Pressure on housing, water and services. (ii) Availability of cheap labour and cultural diversity. (iii) Possible growth of slums and social tensions if planning is poor.

questions.text: In a town, there are 52,000 males and 49,400 females. Calculate the sex ratio.
questions.answer: Sex ratio = (49,400 ÷ 52,000) × 1000 ≈ 950 females per 1000 males.

questions.text: The process of movement of population from rural to urban areas is called:
questions.answer: Migration

questions.text: Which of the following is a push factor of migration?
questions.answer: Natural calamities

questions.text: Define migration.
questions.answer: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another for a temporary or permanent period.

questions.text: What is population density?
questions.answer: Population density is the number of persons living per square kilometre area.

questions.text: State the factors affecting population density.
questions.answer: Physical factors like climate, relief and soil and economic factors like industries, transport and urbanisation affect population density.

questions.text: Explain pull factors of migration.
questions.answer: Pull factors include employment opportunities, better education, healthcare, higher wages and urban amenities.

questions.text: Show any two high population density regions in the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned map question image in /public/maps and reference it using imageUrl.
questions.answer: East Asia and South Asia

questions.text: Draw a diagram showing rural to urban migration.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a simple migration flow diagram and save under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Flow of population from villages to cities due to push and pull factors.

questions.text: Explain causes and effects of migration.
questions.answer: Migration occurs due to push and pull factors like poverty, unemployment, education and urbanisation. It affects population distribution, urban growth and socio-economic conditions.

chapters.title: Human Settlements and Land Use
chapters.description: Types and patterns of human settlements, factors affecting their location and growth, land use types, and the relationship between settlements and land use.
topics: Concept and types of human settlements
Factors affecting location and growth of settlements
Concept of land use and land cover
Types of rural and urban land use
learningObjectives: Classify settlements into rural and urban with examples.
Describe different settlement patterns and relate them to physical factors.
Explain major types of land use in rural and urban areas.
Analyse how transport, relief and water availability influence settlement location.
Discuss the need for proper land use planning.

questions.text: A settlement in which houses are closely spaced around a central point like a market or temple is called:
questions.answer: Nucleated settlement

questions.text: Differentiate between rural and urban settlements on any two points.
questions.answer: Rural settlements: mainly engaged in primary activities, low building density and more open space. Urban settlements: mainly engaged in secondary and tertiary activities, high building density and better infrastructure.

questions.text: What is land use? Give two examples of land use in rural areas.
questions.answer: Land use refers to the purposes for which land is used by humans, such as agriculture, settlement, industry or recreation. In rural areas examples are crop cultivation and grazing land.

questions.text: Which of the following factors is most responsible for linear settlements?
questions.answer: Along transport routes or rivers

questions.text: Explain any three physical and any three human factors affecting the location and growth of human settlements.
questions.answer: Physical: (i) Relief – plains favour larger settlements; steep slopes discourage them. (ii) Climate – moderate climate attracts people, extreme climate discourages. (iii) Water – proximity to rivers, lakes and groundwater supports settlements. Human: (i) Transport routes like highways and railways stimulate growth. (ii) Availability of jobs in industries or services. (iii) Government policies such as new town development or relocation schemes.

questions.text: Why do some mountainous regions still have dense settlements despite difficult terrain?
questions.answer: Because they may have valuable resources (minerals, tourism), fertile valley floors, or strategic importance that offers employment and services, attracting population despite harsh relief.

questions.text: Conversion of agricultural land into built-up area is an example of:
options: Both land use and land cover change
questions.answer: Both land use and land cover change

questions.text: In a village, the total area is 500 hectares. Out of this, 300 ha is under agriculture, 50 ha under forest, 100 ha under settlement and roads, and 50 ha is wasteland. Calculate the percentage of land under agriculture and settlement.
questions.answer: Agriculture: (300 ÷ 500) × 100 = 60%. Settlement and roads: (100 ÷ 500) × 100 = 20%.

questions.text: List any two problems created due to unplanned urban land use.
questions.answer: Examples: traffic congestion, slums, shortage of open spaces, pollution, overburdened water supply and drainage systems.

questions.text: Describe the need for land use planning in a rapidly growing city.
questions.answer: Land use planning ensures proper location of residential, industrial and commercial areas, protects environmentally sensitive zones, provides adequate transport and public services, prevents haphazard growth and slums, and helps maintain a balance between development and quality of life.

questions.text: Which of the following is a rural settlement pattern?
questions.answer: All of the above

questions.text: The settlement pattern found along rivers and roads is:
questions.answer: Linear

questions.text: Define human settlement.
questions.answer: Human settlement is a place where people establish their dwellings and carry out economic and social activities.

questions.text: What is land use?
questions.answer: Land use refers to the way land is utilized for various purposes like agriculture, settlement, industry and transport.

questions.text: Explain factors affecting rural settlements.
questions.answer: Physical factors like relief, climate, soil and water availability and human factors like agriculture and transport affect rural settlements.

questions.text: State the factors affecting land use.
questions.answer: Physical factors include relief, climate and soil; economic and social factors include population, technology and government policies.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of compact settlement.
questions.howToSaveImage: Scan or draw a labelled compact settlement diagram and store it under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Houses closely built with common facilities at centre.

questions.text: Show an urban settlement on the map of India.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned India map under /public/maps and mark a major city.
questions.answer: Mumbai / Delhi / Kolkata (any one)

questions.text: Explain types of rural settlements with suitable diagrams.
questions.answer: Rural settlements are compact, linear and dispersed. Each type depends on relief, water supply and agricultural practices.

chapters.title: Primary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature and types of primary activities like agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining, their spatial distribution and recent changes.
topics: Meaning and types of primary activities
Fishing and forestry as primary activities
Recent changes and modernisation in primary sector
learningObjectives: Define primary economic activities with examples.
Differentiate between subsistence and commercial agriculture.
Explain important types of agriculture and their regional examples.
Describe global distribution of fishing, forestry and mining regions in brief.
Discuss problems and changes in primary economic activities.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a primary activity?
questions.answer: Software development

questions.text: State any two differences between subsistence farming and commercial farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence: small land holdings, use of family labour, production mainly for own consumption. Commercial: large farms, hired labour, production for market and profit.

questions.text: What is plantation agriculture? Give two examples of plantation crops.
questions.answer: Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large estate using modern techniques and wage labour; examples: tea, coffee, rubber, oil palm.

questions.text: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Rice – intensive subsistence farming in monsoon Asia
Maize – shifting cultivation crop in Arctic
questions.answer: Rice – intensive subsistence farming in monsoon Asia

questions.text: Explain the factors affecting the development of fishing industry in the world.
questions.answer: Factors: (i) Physical – continental shelf, cold and warm current convergence, nutrient-rich waters. (ii) Climatic – suitable temperatures and absence of storms during fishing seasons. (iii) Economic – demand in domestic and foreign markets, availability of refrigeration and processing. (iv) Technological – modern trawlers, sonar, cold storage. (v) Government policies like subsidies and exclusive economic zones.

questions.text: Mention two major problems faced by farmers in India.
questions.answer: Examples: dependence on monsoon, fragmentation of land holdings, lack of irrigation facilities, low use of modern inputs, low and fluctuating market prices.

questions.text: Mining of which mineral is most important in the Chota Nagpur plateau?
questions.answer: Iron ore and coal

questions.text: A farmer owns 2 hectares of land. On one hectare he grows food grains only for his family, and on the other hectare he grows sugarcane for selling to a factory. Calculate the percentage of his land under subsistence and commercial farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence: (1 ÷ 2) × 100 = 50%. Commercial: (1 ÷ 2) × 100 = 50%.

questions.text: What is shifting cultivation? Mention one region where it is still practised.
questions.answer: Shifting cultivation is an agricultural system in which a plot of land is cleared, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned for another plot; examples: North-East India, Amazon basin, parts of Congo basin.

questions.text: Discuss any three environmental problems created by intensive exploitation of primary resources like forests and minerals.
questions.answer: Problems: (i) Deforestation leading to soil erosion, loss of biodiversity and climate change. (ii) Over-mining causing land degradation, subsidence and pollution of water bodies. (iii) Overfishing resulting in depletion of fish stocks and ecological imbalance in marine ecosystems.

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary economic activity?
questions.answer: Fishing

questions.text: Which type of farming is mainly practised in densely populated regions?
questions.answer: Intensive farming

questions.text: Define primary economic activities.
questions.answer: Primary economic activities involve extraction of natural resources directly from the Earth such as agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining.

questions.text: What is shifting cultivation?
questions.answer: Shifting cultivation is a farming method where land is cleared, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned to regain fertility.

questions.text: State the characteristics of commercial farming.
questions.answer: Commercial farming is market-oriented, uses modern technology, high capital input and produces crops for sale.

questions.text: Explain subsistence farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence farming is practised to meet the needs of the farmer's family using traditional tools and methods.

questions.text: Show major wheat producing regions of the world on the map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map in /public/maps and mark major wheat belts.
questions.answer: North America, Europe, Asia

questions.text: Draw a diagram showing shifting cultivation.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a simple labelled diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Forest cleared → cultivated → abandoned

questions.text: Explain different types of farming with examples.
questions.answer: Farming types include subsistence, commercial, intensive and shifting farming, each with distinct characteristics and examples.

chapters.title: Secondary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature of secondary activities, types of industries, factors affecting industrial location, major industrial regions of the world and emerging trends.
topics: Definition of secondary activities and industries
Classification of industries (size, ownership, raw material, product)
Major industrial regions of the world
learningObjectives: Define secondary economic activities and classify industries.
Explain physical and human factors responsible for industrial location.
Identify major industrial regions of the world and India on a map.
Describe characteristics of footloose and information technology industries.
Discuss environmental problems caused by industries.

questions.text: Which of the following is a secondary activity?
questions.answer: Steel manufacturing

questions.text: State any two factors affecting the location of industries.
questions.answer: Examples: availability of raw materials, power supply, labour, transport facilities, market, government policies.

questions.text: What are footloose industries? Give one example.
questions.answer: Footloose industries are those which are not tied to any specific raw material or market location and can be located in a wide choice of places; example: electronics assembly, software industry.

questions.text: The Ruhr region of Germany is famous for:
questions.answer: Iron and steel industry

questions.text: Explain how market and transport facilities influence industrial location.
questions.answer: Industries producing bulky or perishable finished goods prefer locations near markets to reduce transport cost and ensure quick delivery. Good transport facilities (roads, railways, ports) reduce cost of bringing raw materials and sending finished products, allow easy access to national and international markets and thus attract industries to such nodes and corridors.

questions.text: Mention any two characteristics of high-technology (hi-tech) industries.
questions.answer: Characteristics: high investment in research and development; use of advanced electronics and robotics; highly skilled workforce; clean and environment-friendly production compared to traditional heavy industries.

questions.text: Which one is an example of public sector industry in India?
questions.answer: BHEL

questions.text: In an industrial region, 40% of workers are engaged in engineering industries, 35% in textile industries and the rest in food-processing. If total industrial workers are 2,00,000, find the number working in food-processing.
questions.answer: Percentage in food-processing = 100 − (40 + 35) = 25%. Number = 25% of 2,00,000 = 50,000 workers.

questions.text: List any two environmental problems caused by concentration of industries.
questions.answer: Air pollution from smoke and gases, water pollution from industrial effluents, noise pollution, solid waste generation and land degradation.

questions.text: Describe any three advantages of industrial regions for the economic development of a country.
questions.answer: Advantages: (i) Economies of scale as industries share infrastructure and services. (ii) Large employment opportunities and urban growth. (iii) Development of transport, banking and other services. (iv) Increase in exports and tax revenue, contributing to GDP.

questions.text: Which of the following activities converts raw materials into finished goods?
questions.answer: Manufacturing

questions.text: Cottage industries are generally:
questions.answer: Household based

questions.text: Define secondary economic activities.
questions.answer: Secondary economic activities involve processing of raw materials into semi-finished or finished goods through manufacturing.

questions.text: What is manufacturing?
questions.answer: Manufacturing is the process of converting raw materials into finished products using labour, machines and power.

questions.text: State the factors affecting location of industries.
questions.answer: Availability of raw materials, power, labour, transport, market and capital affect industrial location.

questions.text: Explain small scale industries.
questions.answer: Small scale industries require less capital, use simple technology and employ local labour to produce goods for nearby markets.

questions.text: Show major iron and steel producing regions of the world on the map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map in /public/maps and mark major iron and steel belts.
questions.answer: USA, Europe, China, India

questions.text: Draw a flow diagram of manufacturing process.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a labelled flow diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Raw material → Processing → Finished goods

questions.text: Explain types of industries with examples.
questions.answer: Industries are classified as cottage, small-scale and large-scale based on size, capital, technology and output with examples.

chapters.title: Tertiary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature and types of tertiary activities such as trade, transport, tourism and communication, their interrelationships and changing trends.
topics: Definition and types of tertiary activities
Relationship between trade, transport and tourism
Recent trends: e-commerce, digital services, globalisation
Problems and prospects of tertiary sector in developing countries
learningObjectives: Define tertiary activities and give examples.
Explain the role of transport and communication in economic development.
Differentiate between internal and international trade.
Discuss the importance and impacts of tourism.
Describe how trade, transport and tourism are interlinked.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a tertiary activity?
questions.answer: Road construction

questions.text: State any two advantages of good transport facilities to a region.
questions.answer: They help movement of raw materials and finished goods, reduce transport cost and time, promote trade and tourism and integrate remote areas with markets.

questions.text: Differentiate between internal trade and international trade.
questions.answer: Internal trade takes place within the boundaries of a country and uses national currency, whereas international trade occurs between different countries and involves foreign exchange and customs procedures.

questions.text: Which factor has recently contributed most to the growth of e-commerce?
options: Discovery of sea route to India
questions.answer: Spread of internet and smartphones

questions.text: Explain any three positive and any two negative impacts of tourism on a destination region.
questions.answer: Positive: (i) Generates employment and income. (ii) Develops infrastructure like roads, airports and hotels. (iii) Encourages preservation of culture and heritage. Negative: (i) Environmental degradation due to pollution and littering. (ii) Overcrowding and seasonal pressure on local resources, sometimes cultural commodification.

questions.text: What is meant by globalisation of services? Give one example.
questions.answer: Globalisation of services means services such as IT, banking, education and health are provided across national boundaries using communication technology, e.g., Indian IT companies providing software services to clients in USA or Europe.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.answer: Banking – financial service

questions.text: A country exported goods worth ₹800 crore and imported goods worth ₹650 crore in a year. Calculate its balance of trade and state whether it is favourable or unfavourable.
questions.answer: Balance of trade = Exports − Imports = 800 − 650 = ₹150 crore (surplus). It is a favourable balance of trade.

questions.text: Explain the term 'transport corridor' with an example.
questions.answer: A transport corridor is a well-developed route connecting major centres with concentrated road, rail or water transport facilities, e.g., the Golden Quadrilateral in India connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

questions.text: Describe the relationship between trade, transport and tourism.
questions.answer: Efficient transport connects producers and consumers, enabling trade of goods. Developed trade encourages better transport infrastructure like ports and airports. The same transport networks allow tourists to reach destinations; in turn, growth of tourism justifies further improvements in transport and communication. Thus, trade, transport and tourism support each other's growth.

questions.text: Which of the following is a tertiary economic activity?
questions.answer: Transport

questions.text: Which service helps in movement of goods and people?
questions.answer: Transport

questions.text: Define tertiary economic activities.
questions.answer: Tertiary economic activities provide services that support primary and secondary activities and help people directly or indirectly.

questions.text: What is trade?
questions.answer: Trade is the exchange of goods and services between producers and consumers.

questions.text: State the importance of transport.
questions.answer: Transport connects producers and consumers, promotes trade, supports industrial growth and facilitates regional development.

questions.text: Explain tourism as a tertiary activity.
questions.answer: Tourism involves travel for recreation and generates employment, foreign exchange and infrastructure development.

questions.text: Show major international air routes on the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map under /public/maps and mark major air routes.
questions.answer: North America–Europe, Asia–Europe routes

questions.text: Draw a flow diagram showing interdependence of economic activities.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a labelled flow diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Primary → Secondary → Tertiary activities

questions.text: Explain different types of tertiary economic activities with examples.
questions.answer: Tertiary activities include transport, trade, tourism, communication and services which support economic development.

chapters.title: Region and Regional Development
chapters.description: Concept of region, types of regions, indicators of development, regional imbalance and measures for balanced regional development.
topics: Case examples of regional development programmes
learningObjectives: Define region and explain its characteristics.
Differentiate between various types of regions.
Explain concept of regional development and imbalance.
Identify factors responsible for regional disparities.
Suggest measures for balanced regional development.

questions.text: An area organised around a focal point such as a city and its surrounding hinterland is called a:
questions.answer: Functional region

questions.text: Define 'region' in geographical sense.
questions.answer: Region is an area of the earth's surface that is homogeneous with respect to certain selected criteria such as climate, economy or culture and differs from surrounding areas.

questions.text: State any two indicators used to measure regional development.
questions.answer: Examples: per capita income, literacy rate, level of industrialisation, availability of infrastructure (roads, electricity, health services), Human Development Index.

questions.text: A state boundary in India is an example of which type of region?
questions.answer: Administrative region

questions.text: Explain any three causes of regional imbalance within a country.
questions.answer: Causes: (i) Unequal distribution of natural resources such as minerals, fertile soils or water. (ii) Historical factors like colonial policies favouring some ports and regions. (iii) Concentration of industries and infrastructure in few growth centres while other areas remain neglected. (iv) Political decisions, poor governance or lack of investment in backward regions.

questions.text: What is meant by balanced regional development?
questions.answer: Balanced regional development refers to a situation where all regions of a country develop in a reasonably similar way and no region remains permanently backward or highly deprived compared to others.

questions.text: Which of the following is a measure to reduce regional disparities?
options: Concentrating all industries in one metro city
Providing tax incentives to industries in backward areas
questions.answer: Providing tax incentives to industries in backward areas

questions.text: Region A has per capita income of ₹1,20,000 and literacy rate of 85%. Region B has per capita income of ₹60,000 and literacy rate of 65%. Calculate the difference in per capita income and literacy rate between the two regions.
questions.answer: Difference in per capita income = 1,20,000 − 60,000 = ₹60,000. Difference in literacy rate = 85% − 65% = 20 percentage points.

questions.text: Give two examples of natural regions.
questions.answer: Examples: monsoon region of South Asia, equatorial rainforest region, Mediterranean region, hot desert region (any two).

questions.text: Suggest any three planning measures that the government can adopt to promote development in a backward region.
questions.answer: Measures: (i) Develop basic infrastructure like roads, electricity, irrigation and communication. (ii) Provide special financial incentives, subsidies and tax concessions to attract industries. (iii) Improve education, skill development and health services for local people. (iv) Promote region-specific resources like tourism, horticulture or handicrafts.

questions.text: A region having similar physical and human characteristics is called:
questions.answer: Geographical region

questions.text: Regional imbalance leads to:
questions.answer: Migration

questions.text: Define region.
questions.answer: A region is a specific area of the Earth's surface having one or more common characteristics.

questions.text: What is regional development?
questions.answer: Regional development refers to the process of improving the economic and social conditions of a region.

questions.text: State the causes of regional imbalance.
questions.answer: Unequal resource distribution, lack of infrastructure, uneven industrialisation and poor planning cause regional imbalance.

questions.text: Explain measures to reduce regional imbalance.
questions.answer: Balanced industrial development, infrastructure development, decentralised planning and government schemes help reduce regional imbalance.

questions.text: Show any one developed and one backward region in India on the map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned India map in /public/maps and mark regions clearly.
questions.answer: Developed: Western Maharashtra / Backward: Eastern Vidarbha (any correct example)

questions.text: Draw a diagram showing regional imbalance.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create a simple comparative diagram and save under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Contrast between developed and backward regions

questions.text: Explain the concept of regional development with reference to India.
questions.answer: Regional development in India aims at reducing disparities by promoting balanced growth through planning, infrastructure and industrialisation.

chapters.title: Geography: Nature and Scope
chapters.description: Concept, nature and branches of geography, its relationship with other disciplines, uses and applications of geography in modern times.
topics: Nature of geography as an integrating discipline
Branches of physical and human geography
Relationship of geography with other subjects
Importance and scope of geography in daily life
Use of technology in geography (GIS, remote sensing, GPS)
learningObjectives: Define geography and explain its dual character as physical and human science.
Identify major branches and sub-branches of geography.
Explain how geography is related to other natural and social sciences.
Recognise the practical applications of geography in planning and management.
Appreciate the growing scope of modern tools like GIS and remote sensing.

questions.text: Geography is mainly concerned with:
options: Only physical features of the Earth
Interaction between humans and their environment
questions.answer: Interaction between humans and their environment

questions.text: Name any two branches each of physical geography and human geography.
questions.answer: Physical: climatology, geomorphology, biogeography, oceanography. Human: population geography, economic geography, political geography, social geography (any two of each).

questions.text: What is meant by applied geography?
questions.answer: Applied geography deals with the practical application of geographical knowledge and techniques to solve real-world problems such as urban planning, disaster management, transport planning and resource management.

questions.text: Which technology uses satellites to collect information about the Earth's surface?
questions.answer: Remote sensing

questions.text: Explain how geography is both a physical science and a social science.
questions.answer: As physical science, geography studies landforms, climate, soils, vegetation and processes shaping the natural environment. As social science, it studies population, settlements, economic activities and cultural landscapes. It integrates these aspects by examining how human activities depend on and modify physical environment.

questions.text: Mention two uses of Geographic Information System (GIS).
questions.answer: GIS is used for preparing and analysing thematic maps such as land use, transport networks, disaster risk zones, and for urban planning, route optimisation, environmental management etc.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
questions.answer: Orology – study of trade routes

questions.text: In a GIS project, 4 thematic layers are used: land use, roads, rivers and population density. If each layer is stored as one file of size 250 MB, calculate the total storage required in GB.
questions.answer: Total size = 4 × 250 MB = 1000 MB = 1 GB.

questions.text: How does the study of geography help in disaster management?
questions.answer: Geography provides knowledge of hazard-prone areas, landforms, climate and human settlements; using maps, remote sensing and GIS, it helps in risk assessment, evacuation planning, resource allocation and post-disaster rehabilitation.

questions.text: Describe the importance of geography in your day-to-day life (any five points).
questions.answer: Examples: (i) Helps understand weather forecasts and plan activities. (ii) Guides route selection and travel using maps and GPS. (iii) Explains availability of resources like water and food. (iv) Creates awareness about environmental issues and sustainable use of resources. (v) Helps understand regional cultures and global events. (vi) Useful in careers such as planning, logistics, environment and tourism.

questions.text: Geography is a science that studies:
options: Earth as the home of humans
questions.answer: Earth as the home of humans

questions.text: Which branch of geography deals with landforms, climate and soils?
questions.answer: Physical Geography

questions.text: Define geography.
questions.answer: Geography is the science that studies the spatial distribution and interrelationship of physical and human phenomena on the Earth's surface.

questions.text: What is the scope of geography?
questions.answer: The scope of geography includes the study of physical features, human activities, their interrelationships and spatial patterns on Earth.

questions.text: State the importance of geography.
questions.answer: Geography helps in understanding natural resources, environment, human settlements, regional planning and sustainable development.

questions.text: Explain the relationship between physical and human geography.
questions.answer: Physical environment influences human activities while humans modify the environment, showing a close interdependence between the two.

questions.text: Explain geography as an interdisciplinary science.
questions.answer: Geography integrates knowledge from geology, economics, sociology, environmental science and other disciplines to study Earth holistically.

questions.text: Explain the nature and scope of geography.
questions.answer: Geography studies physical and human phenomena, their spatial distribution and interrelationships, with wide scope covering environment, resources, settlements and regional development.

chapters.title: Advanced Web Designing
