chapters.title: Rotational Dynamics
chapters.description: Uniform and non-uniform circular motion, centripetal and centrifugal forces, banking of roads, conical pendulum, vertical circular motion, moment of inertia, radius of gyration and basic theorems for moment of inertia.
topics: Vehicle on level and banked roads
Moment of inertia and radius of gyration
Theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes
learningObjectives: Describe kinematics of circular motion using angular variables.
Explain centripetal and centrifugal forces with real-life examples.
Apply concepts of banking and friction to calculate safe speeds on curves.
Analyse conical and vertical pendulum motion using energy and force diagrams.
Define and calculate moment of inertia for simple rigid bodies.
Use theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes to find moment of inertia.

questions.text: The force responsible for circular motion of a stone tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle is:
options: Normal reaction of air on the stone
questions.answer: Tension providing centripetal force

questions.text: Define centripetal acceleration and write its expression for a body in uniform circular motion.
questions.answer: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration directed towards the centre of the circular path which changes only the direction of velocity. Its magnitude is aᵣ = v²/r = ω²r.

questions.text: A car of mass 1000 kg takes a turn on a level road of radius 50 m at a speed of 10 m/s. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction required between tyres and road so that the car does not skid.
questions.answer:
Centripetal force = mv²/r = 1000×10²/50 = 2000 N.
Maximum friction = μₛN = μₛmg = μₛ×1000×9.8.
Equate: μₛ×1000×9.8 = 2000 ⇒ μₛ = 2000/9800 ≈ 0.204.

questions.text: A vehicle moves on a smooth banked road of radius 100 m and banking angle 30°. Find the speed at which no friction is required for safe turning (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.answer:
For no friction: v = √(rg tanθ) = √(100 × 9.8 × tan30°)
= √(980 × 1/√3) ≈ √(566) ≈ 23.8 m/s (approximately).

questions.text: What is a conical pendulum? Write the expression for its time period.
questions.answer: A conical pendulum is a pendulum in which the bob describes a horizontal circle while the string traces the surface of a cone. For string length L and semi-vertical angle θ, period T = 2π√(L cosθ / g).

questions.text: A small mass is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1 m using a light string. Find the minimum speed at the highest point so that the string just remains taut (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.answer: At top: T_min = 0, so mg = mv²/r ⇒ v² = gr ⇒ v = √(9.8×1) ≈ 3.13 m/s.

questions.text: Define moment of inertia and write its expression for a system of discrete particles.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass; it measures opposition to change in rotational motion about an axis. For discrete particles: I = Σ mᵢ rᵢ².

questions.text: Moment of inertia of a thin ring of mass M and radius R about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.answer: MR²

questions.text: State the theorem of parallel axes for moment of inertia.
questions.answer: The moment of inertia I about any axis parallel to an axis through the centre of mass is I = I_cm + Md², where I_cm is moment of inertia about the parallel axis through centre of mass and d is the perpendicular distance between the axes.

questions.text: A uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane with angular speed 10 rad/s. Calculate its moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy.
A diver in a swimming pool bends his head before diving. It
questions.answer: Decreases his moment of inertia

questions.text: The angular momentum of a system of particles is conserved
options: When no external force acts upon the system
When no external torque acts upon the system
When no external impulse acts upon the system
When axis of rotation remains the same
questions.answer: When no external torque acts upon the system

questions.text: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal plane with increasing speed. The string breaks because
options: Gravitational force is greater than tension
Required centripetal force exceeds the tension sustained by the string
Centripetal force is less than the tension
Centripetal force is greater than weight of the stone
questions.answer: Required centripetal force exceeds the tension sustained by the string

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a circular loop of radius R about an axis parallel to its diameter at a distance R/2 is
questions.answer: 3/4 MR²

questions.text: A 500 kg car takes a round turn of radius 50 m with velocity 36 km/h. The centripetal force is
A cyclist riding at 14√3 m/s takes a turn of radius 20√3 m. What is his inclination to the vertical?
A string of length ℓ carries mass m and makes 2/π revolutions per second. The tension in the string is
questions.answer: 16 mℓ

questions.text: Find the radius of gyration of a uniform disc about an axis perpendicular to its plane and passing through its centre.
questions.answer: For a uniform disc, I = (1/2)MR², so radius of gyration k = √(I/M) = R/√2.

questions.text: Does the angle of banking depend on the mass of the vehicle?
questions.answer: No, the angle of banking is independent of the mass of the vehicle.

questions.text: During ice ballet, while in the outer rounds, why do the dancers outstretch their arms and legs?
questions.answer: They outstretch their arms and legs to increase moment of inertia and reduce angular speed.

questions.text: State the principle of conservation of angular momentum.
questions.answer: Angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant if no external unbalanced torque acts on it.

questions.text: Two bodies have moments of inertia I and 2I respectively. If their rotational kinetic energies are equal, what is the ratio of their angular velocities?
questions.answer: Since (1/2)Iω₁² = (1/2)(2I)ω₂², the ratio of angular velocities ω₁ : ω₂ = √2 : 1.

questions.text: A hollow sphere has radius 6.4 m. What is the minimum velocity required by a motorcyclist at the bottom to complete the vertical circle?
questions.answer: Minimum velocity v = √(5gr) = √(5 × 9.8 × 6.4) ≈ 17.7 m/s.

questions.text: A bend in a level road has a radius of 100 m. Find the maximum speed of a car without skidding if the coefficient of friction is 0.8.
questions.answer: Maximum speed v = √(μrg) = √(0.8 × 100 × 9.8) ≈ 28 m/s.

questions.text: A flywheel is revolving with a constant angular velocity. A chip of its rim breaks and flies away. What will be the effect on its angular velocity?
questions.answer: When the chip breaks away, the mass of the flywheel decreases, reducing its moment of inertia. To conserve angular momentum, the angular velocity of the flywheel increases.

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc about a tangent in its own plane is (5/4)MR². Find its moment of inertia about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane.
questions.answer: Using parallel axis theorem and perpendicular axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the disc about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is (1/2)MR².

questions.text: Derive an expression for maximum safety speed with which a vehicle should move along a curved horizontal road. State its significance.
questions.answer: The maximum safe speed is v = √(μrg), where μ is the coefficient of friction, r is radius of the road and g is acceleration due to gravity. It signifies that safety speed depends on friction, road curvature and gravity.

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a body about a given axis is 1.2 kg m². Initially the body is at rest. For what duration should an angular acceleration of 25 rad/s² be applied to produce a rotational kinetic energy of 1500 J?
questions.answer: Using K.E. = (1/2)Iω² and ω = αt, the angular acceleration must be applied for 2 seconds.

questions.text: A bucket containing water is tied to one end of a rope 5 m long and rotated in a vertical circle. Find the number of rotations per minute so that the water does not spill.
questions.answer: For no spilling, v = √(rg). The required number of rotations is 13.37 revolutions per minute.

questions.text: A body weighing 0.5 kg tied to a string is projected with a velocity of 10 m/s and moves in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m. Find the tension in the string at the top of the circle.
questions.answer: Using T = m(v²/r − g), the tension at the top of the circle is 38 N.

questions.text: Derive an expression for kinetic energy of a rotating body with uniform angular velocity.
questions.answer: For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω, the rotational kinetic energy is the sum of kinetic energies of all particles: K = 1/2 Σ mi(riω)² = 1/2 Iω², where I is the moment of inertia of the body about the axis of rotation.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the torque acting on a rotating body with constant angular acceleration.
questions.answer: For a rigid body with angular acceleration α, the net torque is the sum of torques on all particles: τ = Σ mi ri² α = Iα, where I is the moment of inertia of the body.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the difference in tensions at the highest and lowest points for a particle performing vertical circular motion.
questions.answer: At the lowest point, TL = mvL²/r + mg. At the highest point, TH = mvH²/r − mg. Using energy conservation, vL² − vH² = 4gr. Hence, TL − TH = 6mg.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the angular momentum of a body rotating with uniform angular velocity.
questions.answer: For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω, the angular momentum is the vector sum of angular momenta of all particles: L = Σ mi ri² ω = Iω, directed along the axis of rotation.

questions.text: A railway track goes around a curve of radius 1 km. The distance between the rails is 1 m. Find the elevation of the outer rail above the inner rail so that there is no side pressure when a train moves at 36 km/h.
questions.answer: Using tanθ = v²/(rg) and h = l sinθ, with v = 10 m/s, r = 1000 m and l = 1 m, the elevation of the outer rail is approximately 1.02 cm.

questions.text: A flywheel of mass 8 kg and radius 10 cm rotates with angular speed 5 rad/s. It is acted upon by a torque of 0.01 Nm for 10 s. Find the change in angular momentum and kinetic energy.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia I = 1/2 MR² = 0.04 kg m². Final angular speed ω = 7.5 rad/s. Change in angular momentum ΔL = I(ω − ω₀) = 0.1 kg m²/s. Change in kinetic energy ΔK = 0.625 J.

questions.text: Two wheels of moment of inertia 4 kg m² rotate at 120 rpm and 240 rpm in opposite directions. If coupled together, find their common speed.
questions.answer: By conservation of angular momentum, the common speed after coupling is 60 rpm.

questions.text: State and explain the theorem of parallel axes.
questions.answer: The theorem of parallel axes states that the moment of inertia of a body about any axis is equal to the sum of its moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through its centre of mass and the product of the mass of the body and the square of the distance between the two axes. Mathematically, I = Ic + Mh², where Ic is the moment of inertia about the centre of mass axis, M is the mass of the body and h is the perpendicular distance between the axes. The proof follows by considering the moment of inertia contributions of all mass elements using the parallel axis geometry.

questions.text: What is a conical pendulum? Obtain an expression for its time period.
questions.answer: A conical pendulum consists of a point mass suspended by a light, inextensible string from a fixed support, moving in a horizontal circle such that the string traces the surface of a right circular cone. If the string makes an angle θ with the vertical and has length L, resolving tension shows that mg = T cosθ and the centripetal force is provided by T sinθ. Using r = L sinθ and v = ωr, the time period of the conical pendulum is T = 2π√(L cosθ / g).

questions.text: Obtain an expression for maximum safety speed with which a vehicle can be safely driven along a curved banked road OR show that the angle of banking is independent of mass of the vehicle.
questions.answer: For a vehicle moving on a banked road of radius r at an angle θ, resolving forces shows that the required centripetal force is provided by the horizontal components of normal reaction and friction. For maximum safe speed, friction reaches its limiting value. The expression for maximum speed is v_max = √[rg (tanθ + μ) / (1 − μ tanθ)], where μ is the coefficient of friction. If friction is neglected, v = √(rg tanθ), showing that the angle of banking depends only on speed, radius and gravity, and is independent of the mass of the vehicle.

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a disc of radius R and mass M about its central axis is:
questions.answer: MR²/2

questions.text: A body performing uniform circular motion has constant:
questions.answer: kinetic energy

questions.text: Define centripetal force.
questions.answer: The force acting towards the centre of a circular path that keeps a body in circular motion is called centripetal force.

questions.text: Define moment of inertia of a rotating rigid body. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia is the rotational inertia of a body about an axis. Its SI unit is kg m².

questions.text: State and prove the principle of conservation of angular momentum.
questions.answer: If no external torque acts on a system, its angular momentum remains constant.

questions.text: An electron revolves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m with speed 3 × 10⁶ m/s. Find its angular momentum.
questions.answer: Angular momentum = mvr = 9.1×10⁻³¹ × 3×10⁶ × 5.3×10⁻¹¹ = 1.45×10⁻³⁴ kg m²/s

questions.text: A torque of 400 Nm acting on a body of mass 40 kg produces angular acceleration of 20 rad/s². Find the moment of inertia.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia I = τ/α = 400/20 = 20 kg m²

questions.text: Derive an expression for the kinetic energy of a body rotating with uniform angular velocity.
questions.answer: K.E. = ½ Iω², derived by summing kinetic energies of particles forming the rigid body.

questions.text: Derive expressions for linear velocity at lowest, mid and top positions of a particle in vertical circular motion.
questions.answer: Using energy conservation, minimum velocity at top is √(gr), expressions follow accordingly.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
chapters.description: Pressure in fluids, Pascal's law, hydraulic devices, atmospheric pressure and barometer, surface tension, capillarity, contact angle, viscosity, streamline and turbulent flow, Bernoulli's theorem and applications.
topics: Streamline vs turbulent flow, Reynolds number
learningObjectives: Explain how pressure varies with depth in a fluid and use Pascal's law in devices.
Discuss atmospheric pressure measurement using a barometer.
Define surface tension and explain related phenomena like capillary rise.
Describe viscosity and distinguish streamline and turbulent flow.
Apply Bernoulli's theorem to simple fluid flow situations.

questions.text: State Pascal's law for fluids.
questions.answer: Pascal's law: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and to the walls of the containing vessel.

questions.text: A liquid of density 800 kg/m³ is filled in a tank. Find the pressure at a depth of 2 m below the free surface (g = 9.8 m/s²).
The rise of liquid in a capillary tube is due to:
questions.answer: Surface tension and adhesion

questions.text: Define surface tension. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid at right angles to a line drawn in the surface. SI unit: N/m.

questions.text: Calculate the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 mm. Surface tension of soap solution is 0.03 N/m.
Differentiate between streamline flow and turbulent flow.
questions.answer: In streamline flow, each fluid particle follows a smooth, well-defined path and paths do not cross; velocity at a point is steady. In turbulent flow, motion is irregular with eddies; velocity and direction change randomly with time.

questions.text: Water flows steadily through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4×10⁻⁴ m² with speed 2 m/s. The pipe narrows to an area of 1×10⁻⁴ m². Find the speed in the narrow portion.
questions.answer: By continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ ⇒ v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ = (4×10⁻⁴×2)/(1×10⁻⁴) = 8 m/s.

questions.text: Using Bernoulli's theorem, explain why the roof of a house may be blown off during a storm when wind speed above the roof is very high.
questions.answer: High wind speed above roof ⇒ high v ⇒ lower pressure above according to Bernoulli (P + ½ρv² = constant). Pressure inside room remains nearly atmospheric. So greater pressure inside pushes roof upward; if force exceeds weight and fixtures, roof may be lifted.

questions.text: The SI unit of coefficient of viscosity is:
questions.answer: Pa·s

questions.text: Define Reynolds number. What does a low value of Reynolds number signify about the flow?
questions.answer: Reynolds number Re = ρvd/η, where v is characteristic speed, d is diameter, ρ is density and η is viscosity. Low Re (typically < 1000) indicates predominantly streamline (laminar) flow.

questions.text: Insect moves over the surface of water because of
questions.answer: Surface tension

questions.text: Water droplets are spherical in free fall due to
questions.answer: Surface tension

questions.text: Surface tension of a liquid at critical temperature is
questions.answer: Zero

questions.text: The unit of coefficient of viscosity is
questions.answer: Ns/m²

questions.text: Two capillary tubes of radii 0.6 cm and 0.3 cm are dipped in the same liquid. The ratio of heights of liquid rise is
The energy stored in a soap bubble of diameter 6 cm with surface tension 0.04 N/m is nearly
Two stones with radii in the ratio 1 : 2 fall from a great height through atmosphere. Their terminal velocities are in the ratio
What is surface film?
questions.answer: A thin layer on the surface of a liquid whose thickness is equal to the range of intermolecular forces is called surface film.

questions.text: What are cohesive forces?
questions.answer: The force of attraction between molecules of the same substance is called cohesive force.

questions.text: What will be the shape of liquid meniscus for obtuse angle of contact?
questions.answer: The liquid meniscus will be convex.

questions.text: What is the net weight of a body when it falls with terminal velocity through a viscous medium?
questions.answer: The net weight of the body is zero.

questions.text: Define velocity gradient.
questions.answer: Velocity gradient is the rate of change of velocity per unit distance between two parallel layers of a fluid.

questions.text: State Stoke's law.
questions.answer: The viscous force acting on a small sphere moving through a fluid is proportional to its radius, velocity and coefficient of viscosity of the fluid.

questions.text: What happens to surface tension at critical temperature?
questions.answer: Surface tension becomes zero at critical temperature.

questions.text: State properties of an ideal fluid.
questions.answer: An ideal fluid is incompressible, non-viscous, its flow is steady and irrotational.

questions.text: Compare streamline flow and turbulent flow.
questions.answer: Streamline flow is smooth with constant velocity at any point, whereas turbulent flow is irregular with eddies and fluctuating velocity.

questions.text: Define surface tension and angle of contact.
questions.answer: Surface tension is the tangential force per unit length acting on a liquid surface. Angle of contact is the angle between the tangent to liquid surface and the solid surface at the point of contact, measured inside the liquid.

questions.text: Calculate the rise of water in a clean glass capillary tube of radius 0.1 mm.
questions.answer: Using h = 2T/(rρg), the rise of water is approximately 0.143 m.

questions.text: A rain drop of radius 0.3 mm falls through air with terminal velocity 1 m/s. Find the viscous force acting on it.
questions.answer: Using Stokes' law F = 6πηrv, the viscous force is 1.017 × 10⁻⁷ N.

questions.text: Two soap bubbles have radii in the ratio 2 : 3. Compare the work done in blowing them.
questions.answer: Work done is proportional to surface area, hence the ratio of work done is 4 : 9.

questions.text: Explain the phenomenon of surface tension on the basis of molecular theory.
questions.answer: According to molecular theory, molecules inside the liquid experience balanced cohesive forces, while surface molecules experience unbalanced inward force, causing the surface to behave like a stretched membrane, producing surface tension.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for capillary rise or fall using forces method.
questions.answer: Balancing upward force due to surface tension and weight of liquid column gives h = 2T cosθ / (rρg).

questions.text: State Stokes' law and give two factors affecting angle of contact.
questions.answer: Stokes' law states that viscous force on a sphere is proportional to radius, velocity and viscosity. Angle of contact depends on nature of liquid–solid pair and impurities.

questions.text: Twenty seven droplets of water coalesce into a single drop. Find the change in surface energy.
questions.answer: The change in surface energy is 1.629 × 10⁻⁷ J.

questions.text: A U-tube with capillaries of different radii shows a difference in meniscus levels. Find the density of the liquid.
questions.answer: Using capillary rise equations, the density of the liquid is found to be 0.8 g/cm³.

questions.text: A rectangular wire frame is dipped in soap solution and the area of the film is increased. Calculate the work done.
questions.answer: Using W = TΔA (considering two surfaces), the work done is 3 × 10⁻⁵ J.

questions.text: Derive the relation between surface energy and surface tension.
questions.answer: Consider a rectangular wire frame with a movable arm dipped in soap solution forming a soap film. Due to surface tension, a force acts on the movable arm. To increase the surface area by a small amount dA, external work dW is done against this force. This work is stored as surface energy. Hence, dW = T dA. Therefore, surface energy E = T × area. Thus, surface tension is numerically equal to surface energy per unit area.

questions.text: Obtain Laplace's law for a spherical membrane.
questions.answer: Consider a spherical liquid drop or air bubble of radius r. Let the excess pressure inside be (P − P₀). If the radius increases by dr, the increase in surface area is dA = 8πr dr. Work done by excess pressure is (P − P₀) × 4πr² × dr. This work is used to increase surface energy T dA. Equating both gives (P − P₀) = 2T / r. This relation is known as Laplace's law for a spherical membrane.

questions.text: Derive an expression for terminal velocity of a sphere falling under gravity through a viscous medium.
questions.answer: Consider a sphere of radius r and density ρ falling through a liquid of density σ and viscosity η. Forces acting are weight (downward), buoyant force and viscous force (upward). At terminal velocity v, net force is zero: weight = viscous force + buoyant force. Using Stokes' law, 6πηrv = (4/3)πr³g(ρ − σ). Solving gives terminal velocity v = (2r²g(ρ − σ)) / (9η).

questions.text: The SI unit of coefficient of viscosity is:
questions.answer: Pa s

questions.text: Viscosity of liquids generally ______ with increase in temperature.
questions.answer: decreases

questions.text: Define viscosity.
questions.answer: Viscosity is the property of a fluid by virtue of which it resists relative motion between its layers.

questions.text: State Pascal's law.
questions.answer: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

questions.text: Explain surface tension.
questions.answer: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting tangentially on the surface of a liquid.

questions.text: Why do liquids rise in a capillary tube?
questions.answer: Due to surface tension and adhesive forces between liquid and tube walls.

questions.text: Calculate excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 mm if surface tension is 0.03 N/m.
questions.answer: Excess pressure = 4T/r = 4×0.03 / 2×10⁻³ = 60 N/m²

questions.text: Find the terminal velocity of a sphere of radius 1 mm falling through a liquid of viscosity η.
questions.answer: Using Stokes' law: v = 2r²(ρ−σ)g / 9η

questions.text: Derive an expression for terminal velocity of a sphere moving through a viscous fluid.
questions.answer: At terminal velocity, gravitational force equals viscous force; using Stokes' law leads to v = 2r²(ρ−σ)g / 9η.

questions.text: Explain Bernoulli's theorem and state its applications.
questions.answer: Bernoulli's theorem states that total energy of a fluid remains constant along a streamline. Applications include lift on airplane wings and venturimeter.

chapters.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
chapters.description: Ideal gas equation, assumptions of kinetic theory, pressure of an ideal gas, mean free path, degrees of freedom, equipartition theorem, specific heats, real gases and van der Waals equation, thermal radiation, black body, Stefan–Boltzmann law and Wien's law.
topics: Ideal gas and kinetic theory assumptions
Pressure and temperature in kinetic theory
Mean free path and collision frequency
Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy
Specific heats of monoatomic and diatomic gases
Real gases and van der Waals equation
Black body radiation and Stefan–Boltzmann law
learningObjectives: State the assumptions of kinetic theory and derive expression for pressure of an ideal gas.
Explain mean free path and factors affecting it.
Use equipartition theorem to calculate internal energy and specific heats.
Distinguish between ideal and real gases and write van der Waals equation.
Describe characteristics of black body radiation and apply Stefan–Boltzmann law.

questions.text: Write the ideal gas equation and define each symbol used.
questions.answer: Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is number of moles, R is universal gas constant and T is absolute temperature.

questions.text: State any two assumptions of kinetic theory of gases.
questions.answer: Examples: (1) Gas consists of a large number of identical molecules moving in random directions. (2) Volume of molecules is negligible compared to container volume. (3) Intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions. (Any two.)

questions.text: Show that average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is (3/2)kT.
questions.answer:
From kinetic theory, PV = (1/3)Nm⟨c²⟩ and also PV = NkT.
Equate: (1/3)Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT ⇒ (1/2)m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT, so average KE = (3/2)kT.

questions.text: What is mean free path? On which factors does it depend?
questions.answer: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a molecule between successive collisions. It depends on number density of molecules, size (diameter) of molecules and temperature/pressure of gas.

questions.text: Using law of equipartition, find molar specific heat at constant volume Cᵥ for a monoatomic ideal gas.
questions.answer:
Monoatomic gas has 3 translational degrees of freedom ⇒ average energy per mole = (f/2)RT = (3/2)RT.
By definition U = nCᵥT for 1 mol ⇒ Cᵥ = (1/U)(dU/dT) = (3/2)R.

questions.text: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature, the approximate ratio Cₚ/Cᵥ is:
Write van der Waals equation for n moles of a real gas and explain the significance of constants a and b.
questions.answer:
Equation: (P + a(n/V)²)(V − nb) = nRT.
Here a accounts for intermolecular attractions (corrects pressure) and b represents excluded volume due to finite size of molecules.

questions.text: State Stefan–Boltzmann law of radiation.
questions.answer: Total radiant energy emitted per unit area per unit time by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: E = σT⁴.

questions.text: According to Wien's displacement law, λₘT = constant, where λₘ is:
questions.answer: Maximum wavelength emitted (peak)

questions.text: The maximum intensity of radiation from a black body occurs at 580 nm. Estimate its surface temperature using Wien's law (b = 2.9×10⁻³ m·K).
The average energy per molecule is proportional to
options: the absolute temperature of the gas
questions.answer: the absolute temperature of the gas

questions.text: The number of degrees of freedom for the vibrational motion of a polyatomic molecule depends on the
questions.answer: structure of the molecule

questions.text: The power radiated by a perfect black body depends only on its
questions.answer: temperature

questions.text: If the absolute temperature of a body is doubled, the power radiated will increase by a factor of
The wavelength corresponding to maximum radiation for a body at 3000 K is nearly
If the ratio of two specific heats of a gas is 1.65, the difference between them is
questions.answer: 7999 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

questions.text: The energy radiated in one minute by a black body of area 200 cm² at 127°C is
Under which condition are Boyle's, Charles' and Gay-Lussac's laws valid?
questions.answer: These gas laws are valid for real gases only when the pressure is low and the temperature is high.

questions.text: On what do the values of absorption, reflection and transmission coefficients depend?
questions.answer: They depend on the wavelength of the incident radiation and the nature of the material.

questions.text: Why does the temperature of a body remain constant at room temperature?
questions.answer: At room temperature, the rate of emission of radiation equals the rate of absorption.

questions.text: Above what temperature do all bodies radiate electromagnetic radiation?
questions.answer: All bodies at temperatures above 0 K radiate electromagnetic radiation.

questions.text: Define root mean square speed of gas molecules.
questions.answer: It is the square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of all the gas molecules.

questions.text: What is black body radiation?
questions.answer: Radiation emitted by a perfect black body which absorbs all incident radiation is called black body radiation.

questions.text: State Wien's displacement law.
questions.answer: The wavelength corresponding to maximum intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature of the body.

questions.text: State factors on which the amount of heat radiated by a body depends.
questions.answer: The heat radiated by a body depends on its absolute temperature, nature of surface, surface area and time of radiation.

questions.text: Show that for a monoatomic gas the ratio of two specific heats is 5 : 3.
questions.answer: For monoatomic gas, Cv = (3/2)R and Cp = Cv + R = (5/2)R. Hence Cp/Cv = 5/3.

questions.text: Show that for diatomic gas the ratio of two specific heats is 7 : 5.
questions.answer: For diatomic gas, Cv = (5/2)R and Cp = (7/2)R. Hence Cp/Cv = 7/5.

questions.text: Show the graphical representation of radiant power of a black body as a function of wavelength.
questions.answer: The graph shows radiant power versus wavelength with a peak shifting towards shorter wavelengths as temperature increases, illustrating Wien's displacement law.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of Fery's black body.
questions.answer: Fery's black body consists of a double-walled hollow sphere with a small aperture, lamp-black coated inner surface and evacuated space.

questions.text: Compare the rate of radiation of a metal body at 727°C and 227°C.
questions.answer: Using Stefan's law, the ratio of radiation is (1000⁴ : 500⁴) = 16 : 1.

questions.text: 1000 calories of radiant heat is incident on a body. If it absorbs 400 calories, find coefficient of emission.
questions.answer: Coefficient of emission = absorbed heat / incident heat = 0.4.

questions.text: A metal cube of side 4 cm radiates heat at the rate of 10 J/s. Find its emissive power.
questions.answer: Emissive power E = Q/(At) = 1041.66 J m⁻² s⁻¹.

questions.text: Show that the root mean square speed of gas molecules is directly proportional to the square root of absolute temperature.
questions.answer: Using kinetic theory and ideal gas equation, vrms = √(3RT/M). Hence vrms ∝ √T.

questions.text: Show that the average energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
questions.answer: Average kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, hence directly proportional to temperature.

questions.text: Calculate the ratio of two specific heats of a polyatomic gas molecule.
questions.answer: For polyatomic gas, γ = (4 + f)/(3 + f), where f is degrees of freedom.

questions.text: Explain the construction and working of Fery's black body.
questions.answer: It is a double-walled hollow sphere with lamp-black coated interior and a small aperture acting as a perfect absorber.

questions.text: Compare rates of emission of heat by a black body at 627°C and 127°C.
questions.answer: Using Stefan's law, ratio = (900⁴ − 300⁴) : (400⁴ − 300⁴) = 37.03 : 1.

questions.text: Determine molecular kinetic energy per mole, per gram and per molecule of nitrogen at 227°C.
questions.answer: KE per mole = 6232 J, per gram = 0.2225×10³ J, per molecule = 1.0335×10⁻²³ J.

questions.text: The velocities of three molecules are 2 km/s, 4 km/s and 6 km/s. Find mean square and root mean square velocity.
questions.answer: Mean square velocity = 18.66 km²/s² and RMS velocity = 4.319 km/s.

questions.text: Explain spectral distribution of black body radiation.
questions.answer: The rate of emission of radiant energy per unit area per unit wavelength of a black body is called spectral distribution. It is studied by plotting radiant power versus wavelength at different temperatures. The curve shows a peak at a particular wavelength which shifts towards shorter wavelengths with increase in temperature, while the total area under the curve increases. This explains Wien's displacement law and Stefan–Boltzmann law.

questions.text: Derive an expression for average pressure of an ideal gas.
questions.answer: Consider an ideal gas enclosed in a cubical box of side L. Molecules collide elastically with the walls. Change in momentum of a molecule on collision with a wall is 2mvₓ. Time between successive collisions is 2L/vₓ. Hence force exerted by one molecule is mvₓ²/L. For N molecules, total force is Nm⟨vₓ²⟩/L. Pressure P = Force/Area = Nm⟨vₓ²⟩/V. Since ⟨vₓ²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3, we get P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩, where ρ is density of gas.

questions.text: Derive Mayer's relation.
questions.answer: Consider one mole of an ideal gas heated at constant volume and constant pressure. At constant volume, heat supplied increases internal energy: dQᵥ = Cᵥ dT. At constant pressure, heat supplied increases internal energy and does external work: dQₚ = Cₚ dT = Cᵥ dT + PdV. Using ideal gas equation PdV = RdT, we get Cₚ dT = Cᵥ dT + RdT. Hence, Cₚ − Cᵥ = R. This is Mayer's relation.

questions.text: The root mean square speed of gas molecules is proportional to:
questions.answer: √T

questions.text: Which of the following laws relates pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature?
questions.answer: Boyle's law

questions.text: Define absolute zero temperature.
questions.answer: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature at which molecular motion ceases, equal to 0 K.

questions.text: State Avogadro's law.
questions.answer: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.

questions.text: Explain mean free path of gas molecules.
questions.answer: Mean free path is the average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions.

questions.text: Why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure?
questions.answer: Because intermolecular forces and finite size of molecules become significant at high pressure.

questions.text: Calculate the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K. (Molecular mass = 32 g/mol)
questions.answer: v_rms = √(3RT/M) ≈ 484 m/s

questions.text: Find the pressure exerted by an ideal gas if number density and mean square speed are given.
questions.answer: Using P = (1/3)ρ⟨c²⟩

questions.text: Derive the expression for pressure of an ideal gas using kinetic theory.
questions.answer: By considering molecular collisions with container walls, pressure P = (1/3)ρ⟨c²⟩ is obtained.

questions.text: Explain black body radiation and Wien's displacement law.
questions.answer: A black body absorbs all radiation. Wien's law states λ_max T = constant.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
chapters.description: Thermodynamic system, variables, processes, first law of thermodynamics, work and heat, specific heats, second law, reversible and irreversible processes, heat engines, Carnot cycle, refrigerator and efficiency.
topics: Thermodynamic system, state variables and equation of state
Isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes
Heat engine, efficiency and Carnot cycle
learningObjectives: Define thermodynamic system and distinguish various thermodynamic processes.
Apply first law to calculate heat, work and internal energy changes.
Use PV diagrams to represent processes and cycles.
Describe second law and limitations on conversion of heat into work.
Explain working of heat engines, Carnot cycle and refrigerator.

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: First law: The heat supplied to a system is used to change its internal energy and to do work on the surroundings: ΔQ = ΔU + W.

questions.text: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas:
questions.answer: Temperature remains constant

questions.text: Distinguish between isochoric and isobaric processes.
questions.answer: Isochoric: volume constant, so no work is done; pressure and temperature may change. Isobaric: pressure constant, so system expands or contracts; both volume and temperature change.

questions.text: An ideal gas is taken through a process in which 500 J of heat is supplied and 200 J of work is done by the system. Find the change in internal energy.
State Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: It is impossible to construct a device operating in a cycle that converts all the heat absorbed from a single reservoir completely into work without any other effect.

questions.text: A heat engine absorbs 1000 J of heat from a source and rejects 600 J to the sink in one cycle. Calculate the efficiency of the engine.
questions.answer: Work done W = Q₁ − Q₂ = 1000 − 600 = 400 J. Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 400/1000 = 0.4 = 40%.

questions.text: A Carnot engine operates between 600 K and 300 K. Calculate its efficiency. If it absorbs 900 J of heat from the source, how much work does it perform?
Define coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator.
questions.answer: COP of a refrigerator is the ratio of heat removed from the cold reservoir per cycle to the work done on the system per cycle: COP = Q₂/W.

questions.text: In an adiabatic process for an ideal gas:
options: No heat is exchanged with surroundings
questions.answer: No heat is exchanged with surroundings

questions.text: Explain with a labelled PV diagram the working of a Carnot engine and derive the expression for its efficiency in terms of source and sink temperatures.
questions.answer: Answer should include: description of four reversible steps (isothermal expansion at T₁, adiabatic expansion T₁→T₂, isothermal compression at T₂, adiabatic compression T₂→T₁); PV diagram showing cycle; use of first law for isothermals giving Q₁ and Q₂; derivation η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁ for ideal gas.

questions.text: When the energy is transferred to a system from its environment,
questions.answer: system gains energy

questions.text: Which of the following system freely allows exchange of energy and matter with its environment?
questions.answer: Open

questions.text: Two systems at the same temperature are said to be in
questions.answer: thermal equilibrium

questions.text: For work done to be reversible, the process should be
questions.answer: cyclic

questions.text: A gas in a closed container is heated with 10 J of energy and does 6 J of work. What is the change in internal energy?
questions.answer: 4 J

questions.text: The second law of thermodynamics deals with transfer of
questions.answer: heat

questions.text: Heating a gas in a constant volume container is an example of which process?
questions.answer: isochoric

questions.text: When are two objects said to be in thermal equilibrium?
questions.answer: Two objects are said to be in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature.

questions.text: What is the science of measuring temperature called?
questions.answer: The science of measuring temperature is called thermometry.

questions.text: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.

questions.text: What is the energy associated with random motion of molecules called?
questions.answer: The energy associated with random motion of molecules is called internal energy.

questions.text: What is a thermodynamic system?
questions.answer: A group of objects that can exchange energy with its surroundings is called a thermodynamic system.

questions.text: On what basis are thermodynamic systems classified?
questions.answer: They are classified based on the transfer of heat and matter with the surroundings.

questions.text: What is a thermodynamic process?
questions.answer: A process in which two or more state variables of a system change is called a thermodynamic process.

questions.text: Draw p–V diagram of a reversible process.
questions.answer: In a reversible process, the p–V diagram is a smooth curve showing gradual change of pressure with volume, retracing the same path during the reverse process.

questions.text: Draw p–V diagram of an irreversible process.
questions.answer: In an irreversible process, the p–V diagram does not retrace the same path during reversal and usually shows a sudden change in pressure or volume.

questions.text: Draw p–V diagram showing positive work with varying pressure.
questions.answer: The p–V diagram shows an expansion curve where volume increases and the area under the curve represents positive work done by the system.

questions.text: Draw p–V diagram showing negative work with varying pressure.
questions.answer: The p–V diagram shows compression where volume decreases and the area under the curve represents negative work done on the system.

questions.text: Draw p–V diagram showing positive work at constant pressure.
questions.answer: The p–V diagram is a horizontal straight line showing increase in volume at constant pressure, indicating positive work.

questions.text: Three moles of a gas at 400 K expand isothermally from 4 L to 8 L. Find the work done.
questions.answer: Using W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁), the work done by the gas is 6.913 kJ.

questions.text: An ideal gas is adiabatically compressed to one-tenth of its initial volume. Find the final pressure.
questions.answer: Using P₁V₁ᵞ = P₂V₂ᵞ, the final pressure is 25.37 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.text: Explain cyclic process.
questions.answer: A cyclic process is a thermodynamic process in which the system returns to its initial state and the net change in internal energy is zero.

questions.text: Differentiate between reversible and irreversible processes.
questions.answer: A reversible process can be retraced in the opposite direction with no energy loss, while an irreversible process cannot be retraced and involves dissipation of energy due to friction or other losses.

questions.text: State the assumptions made for thermodynamic processes.
questions.answer: Thermodynamic processes are assumed to be quasi-static, involve ideal gases, occur under equilibrium conditions, and obey the ideal gas equation.

questions.text: Classify and explain thermodynamic systems.
questions.answer: Thermodynamic systems are classified as open, closed and isolated based on the exchange of heat and matter with surroundings.

questions.text: Explain cases related to energy transfer between system and surroundings.
questions.answer: If Ts < Te, energy enters the system (Q > 0). If Ts > Te, energy leaves the system (Q < 0). If Ts = Te, no energy transfer occurs (Q = 0).

questions.text: Explain the different ways through which internal energy of a system can be changed.
questions.answer: Internal energy can be changed by heat transfer due to temperature difference or by doing work on or by the system.

questions.text: Write a note on thermodynamic equilibrium.
questions.answer: A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when it simultaneously satisfies thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium.

questions.text: Explain graphically positive and negative work in thermodynamic processes.
questions.answer: Positive work is represented by expansion curves on p–V diagram, while negative work is represented by compression curves.

questions.text: State first law of thermodynamics and derive the relation between change in internal energy, heat and work.
questions.answer: First law of thermodynamics states that when heat Q is added to a system, it is partly used to increase its internal energy ΔU and partly used to do work W. Hence, ΔU = Q − W. If no work is done, ΔU = Q, and if no heat is supplied, ΔU = −W.

questions.text: Explain work done during a thermodynamic process with the help of p–V diagram.
questions.answer: Work done in a thermodynamic process depends on the path followed between initial and final states. It is represented by the area under the p–V curve. Expansion gives positive work, compression gives negative work. Different paths give different work even for same end states.

questions.text: Explain thermodynamics of isobaric process.
questions.answer: In an isobaric process pressure remains constant. The system does work as volume changes and temperature also changes. Heat supplied is used partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work. For isobaric process, Q = nCpΔT.

questions.text: Explain thermodynamics of isochoric process.
questions.answer: In an isochoric process volume remains constant, hence no work is done. All the heat supplied increases the internal energy of the system. From first law, Q = ΔU = nCvΔT.

questions.text: Explain thermodynamics of adiabatic process.
questions.answer: In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged with surroundings (Q = 0). Work done is at the expense of internal energy. For adiabatic expansion internal energy decreases, and for compression it increases. The relation is PV^γ = constant.

questions.text: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of conservation of:
questions.answer: energy

questions.text: In an isothermal process, the temperature of the system:
questions.answer: remains constant

questions.text: Define thermodynamic system.
questions.answer: A thermodynamic system is a specified quantity of matter or a region in space chosen for thermodynamic study.

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: Heat supplied to a system equals the increase in internal energy plus work done by the system.

questions.text: What is an adiabatic process?
questions.answer: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged between the system and surroundings.

questions.text: Why is the efficiency of a heat engine always less than 100%?
questions.answer: Because some heat is always rejected to the sink as required by the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.text: An ideal gas absorbs 300 J of heat and does 100 J of work. Find the change in internal energy.
Calculate the efficiency of a Carnot engine working between 400 K and 300 K.
Derive an expression for work done during an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas.
questions.answer: Work done W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) derived using Boyle's law and integration.

questions.text: Explain the second law of thermodynamics and its significance.
questions.answer: The second law states that heat flows naturally from hot to cold bodies and introduces the concept of entropy and irreversibility.
