chapters.description: Simple harmonic motion (SHM), differential equation of SHM, energy in SHM, damped and forced oscillations, resonance, simple pendulum and related concepts.
topics: Simple harmonic motion and restoring force
learningObjectives: Identify SHM and write its displacement equation.
Use differential equation approach to describe SHM.
Calculate velocity, acceleration and energy of a SHM at different positions.
Describe damped and forced oscillations and the phenomenon of resonance.
Derive expression for time period of a simple pendulum.

questions.text: Define simple harmonic motion and give one example.
questions.answer: SHM is oscillatory motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and always directed towards mean position. Example: small oscillations of a simple pendulum.

questions.text: In SHM, acceleration is:
options: Directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction
questions.answer: Directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction

questions.text: A particle performing SHM has amplitude 0.05 m and time period 2 s. Write its displacement equation if at t = 0, it is at mean position and moving in positive direction.
questions.answer:
Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = π rad/s.
Since x(0) = 0 and motion towards +ve, x = A sin(ωt) ⇒ x = 0.05 sin(πt) m.

questions.text: For a SHM, maximum speed is 0.4 m/s and amplitude is 0.08 m. Find its angular frequency and time period.
Write the expressions for potential and kinetic energy of a particle executing SHM.
questions.answer: For mass m, angular frequency ω and displacement x: potential energy U = (1/2)kx = (1/2)mω²x²; kinetic energy K = (1/2)m(v²) = (1/2)mω²(A² − x²).

questions.text: What is damping? Give one example of damped oscillations.
questions.answer: Damping is reduction in amplitude of oscillations with time due to resistive forces. Example: oscillations of a pendulum in air, vibrating tuning fork in air, etc.

questions.text: Define resonance. State one useful and one harmful effect of resonance.
questions.answer: Resonance is the phenomenon in which a system oscillates with large amplitude when driven by a periodic force of frequency close to its natural frequency. Useful: tuning in radio, resonance in musical instruments. Harmful: collapse of structures like bridges when forced near natural frequency.

questions.text: Derive the expression for time period of a simple pendulum executing small oscillations.
questions.answer: For small angle θ, restoring torque ≈ −mglθ, and angular acceleration θ¨ = −(g/l)θ ⇒ SHM with ω = √(g/l). Therefore T = 2π√(l/g). (Steps showing small angle approximation and SHM form should be included.)

questions.text: A simple pendulum of length 1 m has time period 2.0 s. Find its acceleration due to gravity from this data.
questions.answer: T = 2π√(l/g) ⇒ g = 4π²l/T² = 4π²×1 / 4 = π² ≈ 9.87 m/s².

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT change when damping is introduced in a weakly damped oscillator?
questions.answer: Frequency (approximately)

questions.text: A particle is moving in a circle with uniform speed. Its motion is
questions.answer: Periodic but not simple harmonic

questions.text: A particle performing simple harmonic motion with amplitude A and angular velocity ω. The ratio of maximum velocity to maximum acceleration is
Acceleration of a particle executing S.H.M. at its mean position is
questions.answer: Is zero

questions.text: In a seconds pendulum, mass of bob is 50 g. If it is replaced by 100 g mass, then its period will be
questions.answer: 2 s

questions.text: The maximum speed of a particle executing S.H.M. is 10 m/s and maximum acceleration is 31.4 m/s². Its periodic time is
questions.answer: 2 s

questions.text: When the displacement of a simple harmonic oscillator is half of its amplitude, its total energy is
Two S.H.M.s have zero phase difference and equal amplitudes A. The resultant amplitude of their composition will be
questions.answer: 2A

questions.text: A simple pendulum moves from one end to the other in 1/4 second. What is its frequency?
questions.answer: Time from one extreme to the other is T/2. Hence T = 1/2 s and frequency = 2 Hz.

questions.text: A particle executes S.H.M. of 2 cm. At the extreme position, the force is 4 N. What is the force at a point midway between mean and extreme positions?
questions.answer: Force is proportional to displacement. Hence force at midway position is 2 N.

questions.text: A simple pendulum is inside a spacecraft. What will be its periodic time?
questions.answer: Acceleration due to gravity is zero inside spacecraft, hence time period is infinite.

questions.text: What is amplitude of S.H.M.?
questions.answer: The maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position is called amplitude.

questions.text: What is seconds pendulum?
questions.answer: A simple pendulum whose time period is two seconds is called a seconds pendulum.

questions.text: State the formula for frequency of S.H.M. in terms of force constant.
questions.answer: Frequency of S.H.M. is given by n = (1/2π)√(k/m).

questions.text: What does the phase π/2 indicate in linear S.H.M.?
questions.answer: Phase π/2 indicates that the particle is at the positive extreme position during first oscillation.

questions.text: A particle is performing S.H.M. of amplitude 5 cm and period of 2 s. Find the speed of the particle at a point where its acceleration is half of its maximum value.
questions.answer: Using a = ω²x and v = ω√(A² − x²), the speed of the particle is 13.6 × 10⁻² m/s.

questions.text: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of moon is 1.7 m/s². What is the time period of a simple pendulum on the surface of moon if its time period on earth is 3.5 s?
questions.answer: Using T ∝ 1/√g, the time period of the pendulum on moon is 8.4 s.

questions.text: The total energy of a body of mass 2 kg performing S.H.M. is 40 J. Find its speed while crossing the centre of the path.
questions.answer: Using E = 1/2 mv² at mean position, the speed is 6.324 m/s.

questions.text: Derive the differential equation of linear S.H.M.
questions.answer: In linear S.H.M., restoring force F = −kx. Using F = ma, we get d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0, which is the differential equation of linear S.H.M.

questions.text: Define linear S.H.M.
questions.answer: Linear S.H.M. is defined as the periodic motion of a body in which the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it.

questions.text: State any two laws of simple pendulum.
questions.answer: The time period of a simple pendulum is directly proportional to the square root of its length and inversely proportional to the square root of acceleration due to gravity.

questions.text: The period of oscillation of a simple pendulum increases by 20% when its length is increased by 44 cm. Find its initial length.
questions.answer: Using T ∝ √L, the initial length of the pendulum is 1 m.

questions.text: A particle performing S.H.M. has velocities of 8 cm/s and 6 cm/s at displacements of 3 cm and 4 cm respectively. Calculate the amplitude and period of S.H.M.
questions.answer: The amplitude of S.H.M. is 5 cm and the period is 3.14 s.

questions.text: A particle performs linear S.H.M. of period 4 s and amplitude 4 cm. Find the time taken by it to travel a distance of 1 cm from the positive extreme position.
questions.answer: Using x = A sin(ωt + φ), the time taken is 0.46 s.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for resultant amplitude of composition of two S.H.M.s having same period along the same path.
questions.answer: The resultant amplitude R is given by R = √(A₁² + A₂² + 2A₁A₂ cos(φ₁ − φ₂)).

questions.text: Define angular S.H.M. and obtain its differential equation.
questions.answer: In angular S.H.M., restoring torque is proportional to angular displacement. The differential equation is d²θ/dt² + ω²θ = 0.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the period of a magnet vibrating in a uniform magnetic field performing S.H.M.
questions.answer: The time period of vibration of the magnet is given by T = 2π√(I / μB).

questions.text: Using differential equation of linear S.H.M., obtain expressions for acceleration, velocity and displacement of simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: From the differential equation d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0, acceleration is a = −ω²x. Integrating with respect to displacement gives v² = ω²(A² − x²), hence v = ω√(A² − x²). Further integration gives displacement x = A sin(ωt + φ), where A is amplitude and φ is phase constant.

questions.text: Define ideal simple pendulum and obtain an expression for its time period.
questions.answer: An ideal simple pendulum consists of a point mass suspended by a light, inextensible string from a rigid support. For small angular displacement, the restoring force is proportional to displacement, leading to S.H.M. The time period is T = 2π√(L/g), where L is length and g is acceleration due to gravity.

questions.text: Deduce expressions for kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy of a particle performing S.H.M. State the factors on which total energy depends.
questions.answer: For a particle in S.H.M., kinetic energy is Ek = 1/2 mω²(A² − x²), potential energy is Ep = 1/2 mω²x², and total energy E = Ek + Ep = 1/2 mω²A². Total energy depends on mass of the particle, square of amplitude, square of frequency and force constant.

questions.text: Define angular S.H.M. and obtain its differential equation.
questions.answer: Angular S.H.M. is oscillatory motion in which restoring torque is proportional to angular displacement and directed towards equilibrium. Using τ = −cθ and τ = Iα, we get I d²θ/dt² + cθ = 0, which is the differential equation of angular S.H.M.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the period of a magnet vibrating in a uniform magnetic field performing S.H.M.
questions.answer: For a bar magnet of magnetic moment μ suspended in a uniform magnetic field B, the restoring torque is τ = −μBθ. Using I d²θ/dt² = −μBθ, the motion is angular S.H.M. The time period is T = 2π√(I / μB), where I is moment of inertia.

questions.text: The SI unit of angular frequency is:
questions.answer: rad s⁻¹

questions.text: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on:
questions.answer: length of pendulum

questions.text: Define simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: Simple harmonic motion is a periodic motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and acts towards the mean position.

questions.text: Write the expression for time period of a simple pendulum.
questions.answer: T = 2π√(l/g)

questions.text: What is angular frequency? Give its relation with time period.
questions.answer: Angular frequency ω = 2π/T

questions.text: Why is the motion of a simple pendulum approximately SHM for small oscillations?
questions.answer: For small angles, sinθ ≈ θ, making restoring force proportional to displacement.

questions.text: Find the time period of a simple pendulum of length 1 m. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A particle executes SHM with frequency 2 Hz. Find its angular frequency.
questions.answer: ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s

questions.text: Derive the expression for time period of a simple pendulum.
questions.answer: Using torque and small-angle approximation, T = 2π√(l/g) is derived.

questions.text: Obtain expressions for velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM.
questions.answer: v = ω√(A² − x²) and a = −ω²x

chapters.title: Superposition of Waves
chapters.description: Progressive waves, principle of superposition, interference of waves, formation of stationary waves in strings and pipes, beats and their applications.
topics: Stationary waves in strings and air columns
learningObjectives: Describe progressive waves and their basic properties.
Apply the principle of superposition for wave pulses and continuous waves.
Distinguish between constructive and destructive interference and calculate resultant amplitude.
Explain formation of stationary waves in strings and air columns.
Define beats and determine beat frequency in simple situations.

questions.text: In a progressive mechanical wave, which of the following is transferred?
questions.answer: Only energy and momentum

questions.text: State the principle of superposition of waves.
questions.answer: When two or more waves overlap in space, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of displacements due to each wave acting independently.

questions.text: Two waves of amplitudes 3 cm and 4 cm superpose in phase. Find the resultant amplitude and resultant intensity (in terms of I₀, the intensity due to 1 cm amplitude).
questions.answer: Resultant amplitude A = 3 + 4 = 7 cm. Intensity ∝ A², so I = 7² I₀ = 49 I₀.

questions.text: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. What is the beat frequency? How much time is required between successive maxima of sound intensity?
questions.answer: Beat frequency = |260 − 256| = 4 Hz. Time between successive maxima = 1/4 s = 0.25 s.

questions.text: What are stationary waves? State one condition for their formation on a stretched string.
questions.answer: Stationary waves are waves in which certain points (nodes) have zero displacement and others (antinodes) have maximum displacement, with no net energy transfer along the medium. They form when two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose, usually due to reflection at fixed ends.

questions.text: A string of length 1.2 m is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode with a wave speed of 60 m/s. Find its fundamental frequency.
questions.answer: For fundamental, λ = 2L = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4 m. f = v/λ = 60 / 2.4 = 25 Hz.

questions.text: Two waves y₁ = A sin(ωt) and y₂ = A sin(ωt + π) superpose. Find the expression for the resultant displacement and its amplitude.
questions.answer: Resultant y = y₁ + y₂ = A[sin(ωt) + sin(ωt + π)] = A[sin(ωt) − sin(ωt)] = 0. Resultant amplitude is zero (complete destructive interference).

questions.text: List any two properties of a progressive wave travelling in an elastic medium.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Each particle performs SHM about its mean position. (ii) All particles have same amplitude and frequency. (iii) There is a phase difference between neighbouring particles. (iv) Energy is transported along the direction of propagation.

questions.text: The amplitude of each of two interfering waves is A. Show that the ratio of maximum intensity to minimum intensity in the interference pattern is (I_max / I_min) = ∞ when the amplitudes are equal and nonzero.
questions.answer: Resultant amplitude A_R = 2A for constructive interference and 0 for destructive interference. Intensities: I_max ∝ (2A)² = 4A², I_min ∝ 0² = 0, so I_max / I_min = 4A² / 0 → ∞.

questions.text: Explain the formation of stationary waves on a string fixed at both ends. Derive the condition for the frequencies of the harmonics in terms of string length and wave speed.
questions.answer: A wave travelling along the string reflects from the fixed ends and superposes with the incoming wave. For certain frequencies, nodes form at both fixed ends and standing patterns appear. The distance between adjacent nodes is λ/2. For a string of length L fixed at both ends, allowed wavelengths are λ_n = 2L/n (n = 1,2,3,...). Since v = f_n λ_n, we get f_n = n(v/2L). These are the harmonic frequencies of the string.

questions.text: A standing wave is produced on a string fixed at one end with the other end free. The length of the string
options: must be an odd integral multiple of λ
must be an odd integral multiple of λ/2
must be an odd integral multiple of λ/4
must be an even integral multiple of λ/4
questions.answer: must be an odd integral multiple of λ/4

questions.text: The equation of a simple harmonic progressive wave is y = 5 cos π(200t − x/150). The velocity of the wave is
A man stands symmetrically between two mountains and hears first echo after 1.5 s and second echo after 2.5 s. If speed of sound is 340 m/s, distance between the mountains is
In law of tension, the fundamental frequency of vibrating string is
options: inversely proportional to square root of tension
directly proportional to square of tension
directly proportional to square root of tension
questions.answer: directly proportional to square root of tension

questions.text: The integral multiples of fundamental frequencies are
questions.answer: harmonics

questions.text: An organ pipe of length 0.4 m is open at both ends. Speed of sound is 340 m/s. Fundamental frequency is
questions.answer: 425 Hz

questions.text: The phenomenon in which frequency of a body becomes equal to the natural frequency of driven body is called
questions.answer: resonance

questions.text: A wave is represented by equation y = A sin(Bx + Ct). Given that A, B and C are positive. Can you tell in which direction the wave is moving?
questions.answer: The wave is moving in the negative X-direction.

questions.text: Why wave motion is doubly periodic?
questions.answer: Wave motion is doubly periodic because it repeats itself after equal interval of time and space.

questions.text: What is interference of sound waves?
questions.answer: When two longitudinal sound waves arrive at a point such that compression coincides with compression or rarefaction, the resultant amplitude is maximum; otherwise minimum. This effect is called interference.

questions.text: What are beats?
questions.answer: One waxing and successive waning together constitute one beat.

questions.text: What are harmonics?
questions.answer: Frequencies which are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency are called harmonics.

questions.text: What are overtones?
questions.answer: Frequencies greater than the fundamental frequency are called overtones.

questions.text: State law of length of vibrating string.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency of vibrations of a string is inversely proportional to its length, if tension and mass per unit length are constant.

questions.text: State law of tension of vibrating string.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency of vibrations of a string is directly proportional to the square root of tension, if length and mass per unit length are constant.

questions.text: State law of linear density of vibrating string.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency of vibrations of a string is inversely proportional to the square root of mass per unit length, if tension and length are constant.

questions.text: What is resonance?
questions.answer: Resonance is the phenomenon in which a body vibrates with maximum amplitude when the frequency of external force equals its natural frequency.

questions.text: What are forced vibrations?
questions.answer: Vibrations produced in a body under the action of an external periodic force are called forced vibrations.

questions.text: A violin string vibrates with fundamental frequency of 510 Hz. What is the frequency of first overtone?
questions.answer: Frequency of first overtone = 2 × 510 = 1020 Hz.

questions.text: A string 1 m long is fixed at one end and the other end is moved up and down with frequency 20 Hz. What is the speed of the progressive wave producing stationary wave?
questions.answer: Speed of wave v = nλ = 20 × 4/9 = 8.88 m/s.

questions.text: For a stationary wave set up in a string having both ends fixed, what is the ratio of the fundamental frequency to the third harmonic?
questions.answer: Fundamental frequency n₁ = 1/(2L)√(T/μ) and third harmonic n₃ = 3/(2L)√(T/μ). Hence n₁ : n₃ = 1 : 3.

questions.text: What are stationary waves? Why are they called stationary?
questions.answer: When two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose, the resultant wave formed is called a stationary wave. They are called stationary because the wave pattern does not move and there is no net transfer of energy.

questions.text: Distinguish between overtone and harmonic.
questions.answer: Harmonics are integral multiples of fundamental frequency, while overtones are frequencies higher than the fundamental. First harmonic is the fundamental itself, whereas first overtone is the next higher frequency.

questions.text: State any four applications of beats.
questions.answer: Beats are used for tuning musical instruments, Doppler radar measurements, ultrasound diagnosis, and determining unknown frequencies of sound.

questions.text: Prove that a pipe open at both ends of length 2L has the same fundamental frequency as a pipe closed at one end of length L.
questions.answer: For open pipe, n = v/2(2L) = v/4L. For closed pipe, n = v/4L. Hence both have the same fundamental frequency.

questions.text: How is the frequency of vibrating wire affected if the load is fully immersed in water?
questions.answer: When the load is immersed in water, effective tension decreases due to buoyant force. Hence, frequency of vibration decreases.

questions.text: A sonometer wire of length 1 m is stretched by a load of 10 kg and vibrates with frequency 100 Hz. Find the linear density of the wire.
questions.answer: Using n = 1/(2L)√(T/μ), the linear density μ = 2.45 × 10⁻³ kg/m.

questions.text: Find the amplitude of the resultant wave produced due to interference of two waves given by y₁ = A sin ωt and y₂ = A sin (ωt + φ).
questions.answer: Using principle of superposition, resultant amplitude Aᵣ = √(A² + A² + 2A²cosφ) = 2A cos(φ/2).

questions.text: Show that even and odd harmonics are present as overtone modes of vibration of a stretched string.
questions.answer: In different modes of vibration, the string forms one loop, two loops, three loops etc., corresponding to fundamental, second harmonic and third harmonic. Hence both even and odd harmonics appear as overtones.

questions.text: State and explain laws of vibrating strings.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency depends on length (n ∝ 1/L), tension (n ∝ √T) and linear density (n ∝ 1/√μ) of the string.

questions.text: Two wires of same material and area are stretched on a sonometer. One has mass 1 kg and the other 9 kg. If vibrating length of first is 60 cm, find that of the second.
questions.answer: Using n ∝ √(T)/L, the vibrating length of second wire is 1.8 m.

questions.text: The equation of simple harmonic progressive wave is y = sin[π(4t − x/0.25)]. Find amplitude, frequency, wavelength and velocity.
questions.answer: Amplitude = 1 m, frequency = 40 Hz, wavelength = 1 m and velocity = 40 m/s.

questions.text: A stretched wire is in unison with a tuning fork. When tension is increased by 4%, number of beats heard per second is 6. Find frequency of the fork.
questions.answer: Using beat frequency relation, the frequency of the tuning fork is 156 Hz.

questions.text: Explain the formation of stationary waves by analytical method. What are nodes and antinodes? Show that the distance between two successive nodes or antinodes is λ/2.
questions.answer: When two harmonic progressive waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions, their superposition produces stationary waves. Using equations y₁ = a sin(ωt − 2πx/λ) and y₂ = a sin(ωt + 2πx/λ), the resultant displacement is y = 2a cos(2πx/λ) sin(ωt). Points where amplitude is zero are called nodes, and points of maximum amplitude are called antinodes. The distance between two successive nodes or antinodes is λ/2.

questions.text: Explain the production of beats and deduce analytically the expression for beat frequency.
questions.answer: Beats are produced when two sound waves of nearly equal frequencies and equal amplitudes travel in the same direction. Due to superposition, the resultant intensity varies periodically with time. The beat frequency is equal to the difference between the frequencies of the two waves, i.e., n = |n₁ − n₂|. The periodic waxing and waning of sound intensity is called beats.

questions.text: State and verify the laws of vibrating strings using a sonometer.
questions.answer: The fundamental frequency of a vibrating string depends on its length, tension, and linear density. The three laws are: (1) Law of length: n ∝ 1/L, (2) Law of tension: n ∝ √T, and (3) Law of linear density: n ∝ 1/√μ. These laws are verified experimentally using a sonometer by varying one parameter at a time while keeping others constant.

questions.text: Two waves produced by two vibrators in a medium have wavelengths 2 m and 2.1 m respectively. When sounded together they produce 8 beats per second. Calculate wave velocity and frequencies of the vibrators.
questions.answer: Let frequencies be n₁ and n₂. Given |n₁ − n₂| = 8 and v = nλ. Using λ₁ = 2 m and λ₂ = 2.1 m, solving gives wave velocity v = 40 m/s, frequencies n₁ = 20 Hz and n₂ = 19 Hz.

questions.text: The phenomenon of interference is due to:
questions.answer: Superposition of waves

questions.text: In Young's double slit experiment, bright fringes are formed due to:
questions.answer: Constructive interference

questions.text: State the principle of superposition of waves.
questions.answer: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of individual displacements.

questions.text: What is interference of waves?
questions.answer: Interference is the phenomenon of redistribution of energy due to superposition of two coherent waves.

questions.text: Define coherent sources.
questions.answer: Coherent sources emit waves of same frequency having constant phase difference.

questions.text: Why do interference fringes disappear when one slit is closed?
questions.answer: Because interference requires superposition of waves from two coherent sources.

questions.text: Calculate fringe width if wavelength = 600 nm, distance between slits = 0.5 mm and screen distance = 1 m.
Find the position of the first dark fringe in YDSE.
questions.answer: First dark fringe occurs at path difference λ/2 from central maximum.

questions.text: Explain Young's double slit experiment with necessary theory.
questions.answer: YDSE demonstrates wave nature of light by forming alternate bright and dark fringes due to interference.

questions.text: Derive expression for fringe width in Young's double slit experiment.
questions.answer: Fringe width β = λD/d derived using path difference and constructive interference condition.

chapters.title: Wave Optics
chapters.description: Wave nature of light, Huygens' principle, interference, diffraction, polarization and resolving power of optical instruments based on wave theory of light.
topics: Polarization and types of polarized light
learningObjectives: Explain the need for wave theory of light and state Huygens' principle.
Describe coherent sources and conditions for sustained interference.
Use Young's double-slit experiment formula to find fringe width and wavelength.
Explain diffraction patterns and factors affecting fringe width and intensity.
Describe plane polarization and applications of polarizing devices.

questions.text: In Young's double-slit experiment, fringe width is directly proportional to:
questions.answer: Wavelength and distance to screen

questions.text: What is meant by coherent sources of light?
questions.answer: Coherent sources are two or more sources that emit light waves of the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them.

questions.text: In a double-slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 2 m away. If the fringe width is 2.4 mm, calculate the wavelength of light used.
State Malus' law for polarization of light.
questions.answer: When completely plane-polarized light is incident on an analyser, the transmitted intensity I is given by I = I₀ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the transmission directions of the polarizer and analyser.

questions.text: Light of intensity I₀ is incident on two ideal polarizers. The angle between their transmission axes is 60°. Find the transmitted intensity.
questions.answer: After first polarizer intensity is I₀/2. After second, I = (I₀/2) cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8.

questions.text: Differentiate between interference and diffraction of light (any two points).
questions.answer: Interference: due to superposition of waves from two or more coherent sources; fringe width is uniform; occurs over entire screen. Diffraction: due to bending of light around edges/apertures; fringes are generally not equally spaced; usually produced by a single aperture or obstacle.

questions.text: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, the first minimum is observed at an angle of 30′ (30 minutes) when light of wavelength 500 nm is used. Estimate the slit width.
What is meant by resolving power of a telescope?
questions.answer: Resolving power is the ability of a telescope to distinguish two closely spaced point objects as separate. Quantitatively it is the reciprocal of the angular separation of the just-resolved images.

questions.text: Explain how Young's double-slit experiment supports the wave nature of light.
questions.answer: In YDSE, light from a single source is split into two coherent waves, which superpose on the screen to produce alternating bright and dark fringes. Bright fringes correspond to constructive interference and dark fringes to destructive interference. Such a stable interference pattern can arise only when light behaves as a wave capable of superposition; corpuscular theory cannot explain the regular pattern of maxima and minima in intensity.

questions.text: State Huygens' principle. Using it, briefly explain the laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer: Huygens' principle: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront at a later time is the common tangent (envelope) to these secondary wavelets. For reflection from a plane mirror, incident and reflected wavefronts make equal angles with the reflecting surface, and the construction using secondary wavelets shows that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and that the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

questions.text: When light travels from an optically rarer medium to an optically denser medium, the speed decreases because of change in
questions.answer: Wavelength

questions.text: Light of wavelength 5000 Å falls on a plane reflecting surface. The frequency of reflected light is
questions.answer: 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz

questions.text: Light shows wave nature because
options: light travels in a straight line
light exhibits the phenomenon of reflection and refraction
light exhibits the phenomenon of interference
light exhibits the phenomenon of photoelectric effect
questions.answer: light exhibits the phenomenon of interference

questions.text: Young's double slit experiment is carried out using green, red and blue light one colour at a time. The fringe widths recorded are WG, WR and WB respectively then
questions.answer: WR > WG > WB

questions.text: The path difference between two waves meeting at a point is (11/4)λ. The phase difference between the two waves is
Which of the following cannot produce two coherent sources?
questions.answer: Prism

questions.text: The bending of beam of light around corners of obstacle is called
questions.answer: Diffraction

questions.text: In a single slit diffraction pattern, first minima obtained with red light of wavelength 6600 Å coincides with first maxima of some other wavelength. The other wavelength is
What is the shape of the wavefront on Earth for sunlight?
questions.answer: The wavefront of sunlight on Earth is plane.

questions.text: In Young's double slit experiment, if there is no initial phase difference between the light from the two slits, a point on the screen corresponds to the 5th minimum. What is the path difference?
questions.answer: Path difference Δl = (2n − 1)λ/2 = (2×5 − 1)λ/2 = 9λ/2.

questions.text: Two coherent sources whose intensity ratio is 25:1 produce interference fringes. Calculate the ratio of amplitudes of light waves coming from the sources.
questions.answer: Ratio of amplitudes = √(I₁/I₂) = √(25/1) = 5:1.

questions.text: Why two light sources must be of equal intensity to obtain a well-defined interference pattern?
questions.answer: Because the intensity of dark fringes becomes zero and contrast between bright and dark fringes becomes maximum.

questions.text: What is the relation between phase difference and optical path in terms of speed of light in vacuum?
questions.answer: Phase difference Δφ = (ω/c) × optical path.

questions.text: What should be the slit width to obtain pronounced diffraction with a single slit illuminated by light of wavelength λ?
questions.answer: The slit width should be of the order of wavelength λ.

questions.text: What must be the ratio of slit width to the wavelength for a single slit, to have the first diffraction maximum at 45°?
questions.answer: The ratio of slit width to wavelength is √2 : 1.

questions.text: What are secondary sources? State Huygens' principle.
questions.answer: Secondary sources are those sources which do not produce light of their own but emit light received from another source. According to Huygens' principle, every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets which travel in all directions with the same speed as the wave.

questions.text: A plane wavefront of light of wavelength 5500 Å is incident on a double slit arrangement. The total separation of 10 bright fringes on a screen 2 m away is 2 cm. Find the distance between the two slits.
questions.answer: Using W = λD/d, the distance between the two slits is 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ m.

questions.text: State any four conditions for obtaining well-defined and steady interference pattern.
questions.answer: The sources must be coherent, monochromatic, of equal intensity, placed close to each other and the slits should be narrow.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled ray diagram of Fresnel biprism experiment.
questions.answer: The diagram shows a narrow slit source, Fresnel biprism producing two virtual coherent sources, and overlapping wavefronts forming interference fringes on the screen.

questions.text: What is optical path length? How is it different from actual path length?
questions.answer: Optical path length is the product of refractive index and actual path length. Actual path length is the physical distance travelled by light.

questions.text: Differentiate between Fresnel diffraction and Fraunhofer diffraction.
questions.answer: Fresnel diffraction occurs when source and screen are at finite distances, whereas Fraunhofer diffraction occurs when they are effectively at infinity using lenses.

questions.text: Compare Young's double slit interference pattern with single slit diffraction pattern.
questions.answer: YDSE gives equally spaced fringes of equal width, while single slit diffraction has a broader central maximum and unequal fringe widths.

questions.text: White light consists of wavelengths from 400 nm to 700 nm. Find the wavelength range when it passes through glass of refractive index 1.55.
questions.answer: The wavelength range in glass is 258 nm to 451.6 nm.

questions.text: The optical path of a ray of light of wavelength travelling 3 cm in glass of refractive index 1.6 is same as that in a medium of refractive index 1.25. Find the distance travelled in the second medium.
questions.answer: The distance travelled in the second medium is 3.84 cm.

questions.text: Explain reflection of light at a plane surface with the help of a neat ray diagram.
questions.answer: Using Huygens' principle, secondary wavelets from the incident wavefront construct the reflected wavefront such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

questions.text: Describe Young's double slit experiment with a neat diagram showing points of maximum and minimum intensity.
questions.answer: In YDSE, two coherent sources produce alternate bright and dark fringes due to constructive and destructive interference on the screen.

questions.text: Explain the experimental setup for Fraunhofer diffraction with neat diagram.
questions.answer: Fraunhofer diffraction uses a monochromatic source, collimating lens, diffracting aperture and focusing lens to obtain diffraction pattern on a screen.

questions.text: The distance between two bright fringes in a biprism experiment is 0.32 mm for wavelength 6000 Å. Find the change in fringe width if wavelength is changed to 4800 Å.
questions.answer: The change in fringe width is 0.064 mm.

questions.text: A parallel beam of green light of wavelength 546 nm passes through a slit of width 0.4 mm. The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 40 cm away. Find the width of central maximum.
questions.answer: The width of central maximum is 1.1 mm.

questions.text: In Fraunhofer diffraction by a narrow slit, the screen is placed at a distance of 2 m. If slit width is 0.2 mm and first minima is 5 mm from central maximum, find wavelength of light.
questions.answer: The wavelength of light used is 5000 Å.

questions.text: Explain the formation of stationary waves by analytical method. Define nodes and antinodes and show that the distance between two successive nodes or antinodes is λ/2.
questions.answer: When two harmonic progressive waves of equal amplitude and frequency travelling in opposite directions superpose, stationary waves are formed. Using y₁ = a sin(ωt − 2πx/λ) and y₂ = a sin(ωt + 2πx/λ), the resultant displacement is y = 2a cos(2πx/λ) sin(ωt). Points where the amplitude is zero are called nodes and points where the amplitude is maximum are called antinodes. From the cosine term, the separation between two successive nodes or antinodes is λ/2.

questions.text: Explain the production of beats and obtain the expression for beat frequency.
questions.answer: Beats are produced when two sound waves of nearly equal frequencies and equal amplitudes travel in the same direction. Due to superposition, the resultant intensity varies periodically, producing waxing and waning of sound. The number of beats per second is equal to the difference in frequencies of the two waves, i.e., beat frequency = |n₁ − n₂|.

questions.text: State and explain the laws of vibrating strings.
questions.answer: The laws of vibrating strings state that the fundamental frequency of a stretched string is inversely proportional to its length (n ∝ 1/L), directly proportional to the square root of the tension (n ∝ √T), and inversely proportional to the square root of its linear density (n ∝ 1/√μ), provided other factors remain constant.

questions.text: The phenomenon of bending of light around obstacles is called:
questions.answer: Diffraction

questions.text: Which of the following waves can be polarised?
questions.answer: Light waves

questions.text: Define diffraction of light.
questions.answer: Diffraction is the bending of light waves around obstacles and apertures comparable to their wavelength.

questions.text: What is polarisation of light?
questions.answer: Polarisation is the phenomenon of restricting the vibrations of light waves to a particular plane.

questions.text: State Brewster's law.
questions.answer: Brewster's law states that tanθB = μ, where θB is Brewster angle and μ is refractive index of the medium.

questions.text: Why is sky light partially polarised?
questions.answer: Because of scattering of sunlight by air molecules in the atmosphere.

questions.text: Find Brewster angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.
Calculate angular width of central maximum in single slit diffraction.
questions.answer: Angular width = 2λ/a

questions.text: Explain diffraction of light due to a single slit.
questions.answer: Single slit diffraction produces a central bright maximum with alternating dark and weaker bright fringes.

questions.text: Explain polarisation of light and its applications.
questions.answer: Polarisation confirms transverse nature of light and is used in sunglasses, photography and glare reduction.

chapters.title: Electrostatics
chapters.description: Electric field and potential due to charges, Gauss's law and applications, capacitors, energy stored, conductors, insulators and dielectrics in an electric field.
topics: Combination of capacitors and energy stored
learningObjectives: Apply Coulomb's law and superposition principle to find electric field.
Use Gauss's law to determine electric field for symmetric charge distributions.
Relate electric potential to work done and field.
Explain behaviour of conductors and dielectrics in electrostatic equilibrium.
Calculate capacitance of simple capacitors and combinations.

questions.text: Electric flux through a surface depends on:
options: Charge enclosed and permittivity of medium
Distance of charge from surface only
questions.answer: Area vector and electric field

questions.text: State Gauss's law in electrostatics.
questions.answer: The net electric flux through any closed surface is equal to 1/ε₀ times the total charge enclosed by the surface: ∬E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀.

questions.text: A point charge of 2×10⁻⁸ C is placed at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.2 m in air. Find the electric flux through the sphere.
Define electric potential at a point. How is it related to the electric field?
questions.answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point, against the electric field. The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: **E = −dV/dr** (in one dimension).

questions.text: The potential difference between two points is 50 V. How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 μC from lower to higher potential?
A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.02 m² and plate separation 1 mm in air. Find its capacitance (ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m).
What is an electric dipole? Define its dipole moment.
questions.answer: An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance. Dipole moment **p** is defined as the product of magnitude of one charge and the separation vector from negative to positive charge: **p = q·2a** (in magnitude).

questions.text: Three capacitors 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series across a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each capacitor.
questions.answer: 1/C_eq = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = (3+2+1)/6 = 1 ⇒ C_eq = 1 μF. Charge Q = C_eq V = 1 μF × 12 V = 12 μC. In series, charge is same on each capacitor: 12 μC on each.

questions.text: How does the introduction of a dielectric slab between the plates of an isolated, charged capacitor affect (i) its capacitance, (ii) its potential difference, and (iii) its stored energy?
questions.answer: (i) Capacitance increases by factor k (dielectric constant). (ii) As charge remains constant, V decreases by factor k. (iii) Energy U = Q²/(2C) decreases by factor k.

questions.text: Using Gauss's law, derive an expression for electric field intensity due to an infinitely long, uniformly charged straight wire.
questions.answer: Consider a long wire of linear charge density λ. Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L coaxial with the wire. By symmetry, electric field E is radial and same at all points on curved surface; flux through end caps is zero. Total flux = E(2πrL). Charge enclosed = λL. By Gauss's law, E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε₀ r), radially outward.

questions.text: A metal foil of negligible thickness is introduced between two plates of a capacitor at the centre. The capacitance of the capacitor will be
questions.answer: Same

questions.text: Capacitance (in F) of a spherical conductor of radius 1 m is
A dipole is placed in a uniform electric field, its potential energy will be minimum when the angle between its axis and field is
questions.answer: Zero

questions.text: If an electron is brought towards another electron, the electric potential energy of the system
questions.answer: increases

questions.text: The work done in carrying a charge Q once round a circle of radius r with charge q at the centre of the circle is
questions.answer: Zero

questions.text: You are given a number of capacitors labelled as 8 μF – 250 V. Find the number of capacitors needed to get an arrangement equivalent of 16 μF – 1000 V.
A parallel plate capacitor with oil between the plates (dielectric constant k = 2) has capacitance C. If the oil is removed, the capacitance becomes
What do you mean by dielectric polarization?
questions.answer: Dielectric polarization is the phenomenon in which dipole moments are induced or aligned in a dielectric material when an external electric field is applied.

questions.text: Which physical quantity has its unit as J/C? Is it a scalar or vector?
questions.answer: Electric potential has unit J/C and it is a scalar quantity.

questions.text: What are linear isotropic dielectrics?
questions.answer: Linear isotropic dielectrics are those materials in which induced dipole moment is proportional to electric field and is independent of direction.

questions.text: What happens to the energy stored in a capacitor if the plates are drawn apart while the battery remains connected?
questions.answer: Energy stored in the capacitor decreases as capacitance decreases when plate separation increases.

questions.text: The mean free path of electrons in a metal is 4 × 10⁻⁸ m. Find the electric field which can give on an average 2 eV energy to an electron.
questions.answer: Electric field required is 5 × 10⁷ V/m.

questions.text: Find the electric potential at the surface of an atomic nucleus (Z = 50) of radius 9 × 10⁻¹³ cm.
questions.answer: Electric potential at the surface is 8 × 10⁶ V.

questions.text: The capacity of a parallel plate capacitor is 10 μF when the distance between its plates is 9 cm. What will be its capacity if the distance between the plates is reduced by 6 cm?
questions.answer: The new capacitance is 30 μF.

questions.text: Explain the principle of a capacitor.
questions.answer: A capacitor works on the principle of electrostatic induction. When two conducting plates are placed close to each other and charged, equal and opposite charges are induced on them, enabling storage of electrical energy.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the electric field intensity at a point due to an infinitely charged plane sheet.
questions.answer: Using Gauss's theorem, the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge is E = σ / (2ε₀), where σ is surface charge density.

questions.text: What are polar and non-polar dielectrics?
questions.answer: Polar dielectrics have permanent dipole moments due to asymmetric charge distribution, whereas non-polar dielectrics have no permanent dipole moment due to symmetric charge distribution.

questions.text: Two capacitors of 2 μF each are connected in parallel and the combination is connected in series with a 12 μF capacitor. Find the equivalent capacitance.
questions.answer: The parallel combination gives 4 μF. In series with 12 μF, equivalent capacitance is 3 μF.

questions.text: Two spheres A and B of radii a and b respectively are at the same potential. Find the ratio of surface charge densities of A and B.
questions.answer: The ratio of surface charge densities is b : a.

questions.text: A dipole of moment p is placed in a uniform electric field E. Find the work done in rotating it from stable to unstable equilibrium.
questions.answer: Work done = 2pE.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the effective capacitance of three parallel plate capacitors connected in series.
questions.answer: For capacitors C₁, C₂ and C₃ in series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃. Hence the effective capacitance is C = 1 / (1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃).

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor.
questions.answer: Energy stored in a capacitor is given by U = 1/2 CV² = 1/2 QV = Q²/(2C).

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor without dielectric.
questions.answer: Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is C = ε₀A/d, where A is area of plates and d is separation between them.

questions.text: Two parallel plate capacitors X and Y are connected in series across 15 V. X has air and Y has dielectric of constant 2. Find potential difference across each.
questions.answer: The potential differences are Vx = 10 V and Vy = 5 V.

questions.text: Find the work done in rotating an electric dipole of moment 3.2 × 10⁻⁸ C·m in a uniform electric field of 10⁴ N/C from stable to unstable equilibrium.
questions.answer: The work done is 6.4 × 10⁻⁴ J.

questions.text: Three point charges +q, +2q and Q are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. Find Q if the total potential energy of the system is zero.
questions.answer: The value of charge Q is −2q/3.

questions.text: Obtain an expression for the potential energy of an electric dipole in a uniform external electric field.
questions.answer: Consider an electric dipole of charges +q and −q separated by distance 2l placed in a uniform electric field E. The dipole experiences a torque τ = pE sinθ tending to rotate it. Work done by an external agent in rotating the dipole from angle θ₀ to θ is equal to the increase in potential energy. Hence, potential energy U = pE(cosθ − cosθ₀). If reference is taken at θ₀ = 90°, then U = −pE cosθ.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric slab introduced between the plates.
questions.answer: Consider a parallel plate capacitor of plate area A and separation d. A dielectric slab of thickness t and dielectric constant k is introduced. The electric field inside dielectric reduces by factor k. The potential difference across plates is V = E₀(d − t) + (E₀/k)t. Hence capacitance C = Q/V = ε₀A / [(d − t) + t/k]. This is the required expression.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the electric potential at a point due to an electric dipole.
questions.answer: Consider an electric dipole with charges +q and −q separated by distance 2l. Let point P be at distance r from the centre of the dipole making angle θ with the axis. The potential due to +q and −q are V₁ and V₂ respectively. For a short dipole (r ≫ l), the resultant potential is V = (1/4πε₀)(p cosθ / r²), where p = q(2l) is dipole moment.

questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is:
questions.answer: Coulomb

questions.text: The force between two point charges varies inversely as:
questions.answer: square of distance

questions.text: Define electric field intensity.
questions.answer: Electric field intensity is the force experienced per unit positive charge placed at a point.

questions.text: State Coulomb's law.
questions.answer: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to square of distance between them.

questions.text: Define electric potential.
questions.answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.

questions.text: Why electric field inside a conductor is zero?
questions.answer: Because charges rearrange themselves on the surface so that the net field inside becomes zero.

questions.text: Calculate force between two charges of 5 μC each placed 10 cm apart in air.
Find electric potential at a point due to a charge of 2 μC placed 1 m away.
Derive an expression for electric field intensity due to a point charge.
questions.answer: Using Coulomb's law, E = kq/r² directed radially outward or inward.

questions.text: Explain electric potential energy of a system of charges.
questions.answer: Electric potential energy is the work done in assembling charges from infinity to their respective positions.

chapters.title: Current Electricity
chapters.description: Electric current, drift of electrons, Ohm's law, resistivity, series-parallel circuits and application of Kirchhoff's laws, meter bridge and potentiometer.
learningObjectives: Define current, current density and drift velocity and relate them.
Use Ohm's law and equivalent resistance formulas in simple circuits.
Apply Kirchhoff's laws to multi-loop circuits.
Explain principle of Wheatstone and meter bridge to determine unknown resistance.
Use potentiometer to compare emfs and find internal resistance of a cell.

questions.text: Kirchhoff's current law is based on the principle of:
questions.answer: Conservation of charge

questions.text: State Ohm's law. Under what conditions is it valid?
questions.answer: At constant physical conditions (temperature, pressure, etc.), the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it (V ∝ I or V = IR). It holds for ohmic conductors within a certain range of temperature and field.

questions.text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Find their equivalent resistance.
The potential difference across a 4 Ω resistor is 12 V. Calculate the current through it and the power dissipated.
State Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL).
questions.answer: The algebraic sum of all potential differences around any closed loop in an electrical circuit is zero, i.e., ΣΔV = 0.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, the balancing length is 40 cm when the known resistance is 5 Ω. Find the value of the unknown resistance.
questions.answer: Let R be unknown. For balance, R / 5 = 40 / 60 ⇒ R = 5 × (40/60) = 5 × 2/3 = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 Ω.

questions.text: Explain how a potentiometer can be used to compare the emfs of two cells.
questions.answer: Connect the potentiometer wire in series with a driving cell and a rheostat. Connect cell E₁ using a galvanometer and jockey, obtain balancing length l₁ where galvanometer shows zero current. Replace E₁ with E₂ and get balancing length l₂. Since no current flows through the cell at balance, E ∝ balancing length, so E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂.

questions.text: Define resistivity of a material. How is it related to conductivity?
questions.answer: Resistivity ρ of a material is the resistance of a conductor of that material having unit length and unit cross-sectional area. Conductivity σ is the reciprocal of resistivity: σ = 1/ρ.

questions.text: A copper wire 2 m long and of cross-sectional area 1×10⁻⁶ m² has a resistance of 0.034 Ω. Find the resistivity of copper.
Derive the relation between drift velocity of electrons and current in a conductor. Hence obtain the expression for electrical conductivity.
questions.answer: Consider a conductor of length L, area A, containing n free electrons per unit volume, each of charge e and drift velocity v_d. Charge passing per second through area A is q = (number of electrons crossing per second) × e = (nAv_d) e. Thus current I = nAe v_d. Comparing with J = I/A gives J = ne v_d. Using Ohm's microscopic form J = σE, we get σ = ne²τ/m (using v_d = eEτ/m).

questions.text: Kirchhoff's second law (voltage law) is based on
questions.answer: conservation of energy

questions.text: When unknown resistance is determined by metre bridge, the error due to contact resistance is minimised by
options: connecting both the resistances only in one gap
interchanging the position of known and unknown resistances
obtaining the null point near the ends of the wire
questions.answer: interchanging the position of known and unknown resistances

questions.text: The SI unit of potential gradient is
questions.answer: V/m

questions.text: Instrument which can measure terminal potential difference as well as electromotive force (emf) is
questions.answer: potentiometer

questions.text: When null point is obtained in the potentiometer, the current is drawn from the
questions.answer: main battery

questions.text: If potential gradient of a wire decreases, then its length
questions.answer: increases

questions.text: Four resistances 4 Ω, 8 Ω, X Ω and 12 Ω are connected in series to form a Wheatstone's network. If the network is balanced, the value of X is
State Kirchhoff's first (current) law.
questions.answer: The algebraic sum of currents at a junction in an electric circuit is zero.

questions.text: State Kirchhoff's second (voltage) law.
questions.answer: The algebraic sum of potential differences and emfs in a closed loop is zero.

questions.text: What is the basis of Kirchhoff's current law?
questions.answer: Kirchhoff's current law is based on the law of conservation of charge.

questions.text: Are Kirchhoff's laws applicable to both AC and DC circuits?
questions.answer: Yes, Kirchhoff's laws are applicable to both AC and DC circuits.

questions.text: Define potential gradient.
questions.answer: Potential gradient is defined as potential difference per unit length of the wire.

questions.text: On what factors does the potential gradient of a wire depend?
questions.answer: It depends on the potential difference between the wire ends and the length of the wire.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of potential gradient?
questions.answer: Volt per metre (V/m).

questions.text: State any one use of a potentiometer.
questions.answer: A potentiometer can be used to measure the emf of a cell accurately.

questions.text: A voltmeter has resistance 100 Ω. What will be its reading when connected across a cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 20 Ω?
questions.answer: The voltmeter reading is 5 V.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, two unknown resistances R and S give a null point at 60 cm from one end. What is the ratio R/S?
questions.answer: The ratio R/S is 3/2.

questions.text: What are the disadvantages of a potentiometer over a voltmeter?
questions.answer: A potentiometer is not portable and direct measurement of potential difference or emf is not possible.

questions.text: Distinguish between a potentiometer and a voltmeter.
questions.answer: A potentiometer has infinite resistance and does not draw current, whereas a voltmeter has high but finite resistance and draws some current.

questions.text: Distinguish between an ammeter and a voltmeter.
questions.answer: An ammeter measures current and is connected in series, while a voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.

questions.text: How do you calculate the shunt required to increase the range n times?
questions.answer: The shunt S required is given by S = G/(n − 1), where G is galvanometer resistance.

questions.text: Define: (i) Electrical circuit (ii) Junction.
questions.answer: An electrical circuit is a closed conducting path. A junction is a point where two or more conductors meet.

questions.text: Calculate the value of shunt resistance when connected across a galvanometer of resistance 18 Ω to allow 1/10 of the current to pass through it.
questions.answer: The value of shunt resistance is 2 Ω.

questions.text: Four resistances 6 Ω, 6 Ω, 6 Ω and 18 Ω form a Wheatstone bridge. Find the resistance connected across the 18 Ω resistance to balance the bridge.
questions.answer: The required resistance is 9 Ω.

questions.text: What is the maximum safe voltage that can be measured using a galvanometer?
questions.answer: The maximum safe voltage depends on the resistance connected in series with the galvanometer and its maximum current capacity.

questions.text: Explain with a neat circuit diagram how you will determine the unknown resistance using a metre bridge.
questions.answer: In a metre bridge, the unknown resistance is connected in one gap and a known resistance in the other. The balance point is obtained using a galvanometer and jockey. The ratio of resistances equals the ratio of wire lengths.

questions.text: State any two sources of errors in metre bridge experiment and explain how they are minimised.
questions.answer: Errors arise due to non-uniform wire and contact resistance. They are minimised by interchanging resistances and obtaining balance point near the centre.

questions.text: What is potential gradient? How is it measured?
questions.answer: Potential gradient is the potential difference per unit length of a potentiometer wire and is measured as K = V/L.

questions.text: Describe how a potentiometer is used to compare the emfs of two cells.
questions.answer: The emfs of two cells are compared by finding their respective balancing lengths on a potentiometer wire. The ratio of emfs equals the ratio of balancing lengths.

questions.text: A cell of emf 1.5 V is balanced by a length of 300 cm of potentiometer wire. Find the emf of another cell balanced at 350 cm.
questions.answer: The emf of the second cell is 1.75 V.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, balance point is found at 39.5 cm. If known resistance is 12.5 Ω, find the unknown resistance.
questions.answer: The value of unknown resistance is 8.16 Ω.

questions.text: The emf of a standard cell is 1.5 V. Calculate the percentage error if a voltmeter reads 1.8 V.
questions.answer: The percentage error in the voltmeter is 2.857%.

questions.text: Describe with the help of a neat circuit diagram how you will determine the internal resistance of a cell using a potentiometer. Derive the necessary formula.
questions.answer: In this method, a potentiometer wire is connected in series with a cell, key and rheostat. First, the emf E of the cell is measured by keeping the external circuit open and noting the balancing length l₁. Then an external resistance R is connected across the cell and the balancing length l₂ is measured for the terminal potential difference V. Since E/V = l₁/l₂ and V = ER/(R + r), we get r = R(l₁/l₂ − 1), where r is the internal resistance of the cell.

questions.text: Describe how a potentiometer is used to compare the emfs of two cells by the combination (sum and difference) method.
questions.answer: In the sum method, the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the other so that their emfs add. The balancing length l₁ is obtained. In the difference method, like terminals are connected together so that emfs oppose each other and balancing length l₂ is obtained. If E₁ and E₂ are emfs of the two cells, then (E₁ + E₂)/(E₁ − E₂) = l₁/l₂. Solving this gives the ratio of emfs of the two cells.

questions.text: State the uses of a potentiometer. Why is a potentiometer preferred over a voltmeter for measuring emf?
questions.answer: Uses of a potentiometer include measuring emf of a cell, comparing emfs of two cells, determining internal resistance of a cell, and acting as a voltage divider or audio control. A potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter because it measures emf without drawing current from the source, is more sensitive, and provides more accurate results than a voltmeter.

questions.text: The SI unit of electric current is:
questions.answer: Ampere

questions.text: Ohm's law relates:
questions.answer: Voltage and current

questions.text: Define electric current.
questions.answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.

questions.text: State Ohm's law.
questions.answer: At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

questions.text: Define resistance and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current. Its SI unit is ohm.

questions.text: Why are alloys used for making standard resistances?
questions.answer: Because alloys have high resistivity and low temperature coefficient of resistance.

questions.text: Find the current flowing through a conductor of resistance 10 Ω when potential difference applied is 20 V.
Calculate equivalent resistance of two resistances 4 Ω and 6 Ω connected in series.
Derive an expression for equivalent resistance of resistors connected in parallel.
questions.answer: Using Ohm's law and current distribution, 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

questions.text: Explain electric power and derive its expression.
questions.answer: Electric power is rate of electrical energy consumption. P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

chapters.description: Magnetic field of moving charges and currents, Biot–Savart law, Ampere's circuital law, force on a current-carrying conductor, motion of charged particles in a magnetic field and basic ideas of cyclotron.

Motion of charged particle in uniform B-field
Force on current-carrying conductor and torque on coil
Biot–Savart law for straight wire and circular loop
learningObjectives: Compute magnetic force on moving charges and current elements.
Describe uniform circular motion of charged particles in a magnetic field and cyclotron principle.
Use Biot–Savart law to find magnetic field due to current-carrying conductors.
Apply Ampere's law to find magnetic field of solenoid and toroid.
Explain working of a moving-coil galvanometer.

questions.text: The magnetic force on a moving charge is maximum when the angle between velocity and magnetic field is:
State the expression for force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field.
questions.answer: For a straight conductor of length **L** carrying current I in a magnetic field **B**, the force is **F = I (L × B)**. Magnitude F = I L B sinθ, where θ is the angle between L and B.

questions.text: An electron moves with a speed of 2×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.01 T. Find the radius of the circular path. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg)
State Biot–Savart law for the magnetic field due to a current element.
questions.answer: It states that the magnetic field d**B** at a point due to a current element I d**l** is directly proportional to current I, length element dl, sine of angle between dl and line joining element to point, and inversely proportional to square of distance r: dB = (μ₀/4π)(I dl sinθ / r²).

questions.text: Find the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 0.1 m having 50 turns and carrying a current of 2 A.
What is a cyclotron? Name the basic fields used in it.
questions.answer: Cyclotron is a device used to accelerate charged particles to high energies using a combination of a uniform perpendicular magnetic field and a rapidly alternating electric field.

questions.text: Using Ampere's law, show that the magnetic field inside a very long solenoid is B = μ₀ n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length.
questions.answer: Consider a rectangular Amperian loop partly inside the solenoid. Outside field ≈ 0. Line integral ∮B·dl = B·L (inside segment) + 0 (others) = μ₀ I_enc. Current enclosed I_enc = nL I. Thus B L = μ₀ n L I ⇒ B = μ₀ n I.

questions.text: Why is a radial magnetic field used in a moving-coil galvanometer?
questions.answer: A radial magnetic field keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to the field lines so that torque τ = NIAB sinθ is maximum and independent of θ, making deflection proportional to current.

questions.text: A moving-coil galvanometer has a resistance of 50 Ω and gives full-scale deflection for 2 mA. How can it be converted into a 10 V voltmeter?
questions.answer: For full-scale, current I_g = 2 mA. Required series resistance R_s satisfies V = I_g (R_s + 50). So 10 = 2×10⁻³ (R_s + 50) ⇒ R_s + 50 = 5000 ⇒ R_s = 4950 Ω.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current-carrying coil placed in a uniform magnetic field. Define magnetic dipole moment of the coil.
questions.answer: Consider a coil of N turns, area A, carrying current I in a uniform field B. Only the two opposite sides experience equal and opposite forces producing torque. For each side, F = I l B sinθ; torque of pair τ = F·b = I l B sinθ·b = IAB sinθ. For N turns, τ = N I A B sinθ. Magnetic dipole moment is defined as **m = N I A n̂**, so torque is **τ = m × B**.

questions.text: According to right hand rule, the direction of magnetic induction if the current is directed in anticlockwise direction is
questions.answer: perpendicular and outwards

questions.text: A strong magnetic field is applied on a stationary electron. Then the electron
options: moves in the direction of the field
moves perpendicular to the direction of the field
moves opposite to the direction of the field
questions.answer: remains stationary

questions.text: The force between two parallel current carrying conductors is F. If the current in each conductor is doubled, then the force between them becomes
questions.answer: 4F

questions.text: Which of the following is not a unit of magnetic induction?
questions.answer: oersted

questions.text: The magnetic dipole moment of current loop is independent of
options: magnetic field in which it is lying
questions.answer: magnetic field in which it is lying

questions.text: Circular loop of radius 0.0157 m carries a current 2 A. The magnetic field at the centre of the loop is
Magnetic force never does any work on moving charges because
questions.answer: it is perpendicular to velocity

questions.text: What is Lorentz force?
questions.answer: The force experienced by a charged particle moving in electric and magnetic fields is called Lorentz force.

questions.text: What is solenoid?
questions.answer: A solenoid is a long insulated copper wire closely wound on a hollow cylindrical former in the form of a helix.

questions.text: What is toroid?
questions.answer: A toroid is a solenoid of finite length bent into a hollow circular ring.

questions.text: Calculate magnetic field at 2 cm from a current carrying wire of 5 A.
questions.answer: Magnetic field B = 5 × 10⁻⁵ T.

questions.text: What happens to magnetic field at centre of circular loop if radius is doubled?
questions.answer: Magnetic field becomes half of its original value.

questions.text: State the orientation of magnetic dipole for maximum potential energy.
questions.answer: When magnetic dipole and magnetic field are antiparallel.

questions.text: What is SI unit of magnetic field?
questions.answer: Tesla (T).

questions.text: A toroid of 4000 turns has outer radius 26 cm and inner radius 25 cm. If current is 10 A, calculate magnetic field of toroid.
questions.answer: Magnetic field of toroid is 3.137 × 10⁻² T.

questions.text: Why magnetic field lines can be confined within toroid but not within straight solenoid?
questions.answer: Magnetic field lines in a toroid form closed circular paths, whereas in a solenoid they spread outside like a bar magnet.

questions.text: Calculate magnetic field at centre of solenoid of length π m, diameter 5 cm, turns 1000, current 5 A.
questions.answer: Magnetic field is 2 × 10⁻³ T.

questions.text: Two long parallel wires carry equal currents. Find force per unit length between them.
questions.answer: Force per unit length is proportional to I² and inversely proportional to separation.

questions.text: Explain why magnetic force never does work.
questions.answer: Magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, hence work done is zero.

questions.text: State conditions for minimum and maximum magnetic potential energy.
questions.answer: Minimum when dipole is parallel to field, maximum when antiparallel.

questions.text: Obtain expression for magnetic field due to current in circular arc.
questions.answer: Magnetic field B = μ₀Iθ / (4πR).

questions.text: Explain construction and working of moving coil galvanometer.
questions.answer: A moving coil galvanometer works on torque produced on current carrying coil in magnetic field; deflection is proportional to current.

questions.text: Explain Biot-Savart's law.
questions.answer: Magnetic field due to current element is proportional to current, element length and sine of angle and inversely proportional to square of distance.

questions.text: Find magnetic moment and maximum torque of rectangular coil in magnetic field.
questions.answer: Magnetic moment = NIA, maximum torque = mB.

questions.text: Derive expression for magnetic field inside ideal solenoid using Ampere's law.
questions.answer: Magnetic field inside solenoid is B = μ₀nI.

questions.text: Derive expression for torque on rectangular current loop in magnetic field.
questions.answer: Torque τ = NIAB sinθ.

questions.text: Find magnetic field at centre and axis of circular loop.
questions.answer: At centre B = μ₀I / 2R; on axis B = μ₀IR² / 2(R²+z²)³ᐟ².

questions.text: Calculate magnetic moment of circular loop given field at centre.
questions.answer: Magnetic moment m = πR²I.

questions.text: Show that currents in two long parallel wires exert forces on each other. Derive expression for force per unit length.
questions.answer: Force per unit length between two parallel current carrying conductors is F/L = μ₀I₁I₂ / (2πd).

questions.text: Using Biot-Savart law, derive expression for magnetic field due to infinitely long straight conductor.
questions.answer: Magnetic field B = μ₀I / (2πR).

questions.text: Derive expression for axial magnetic field produced by current in circular loop.
questions.answer: Axial magnetic field B = μ₀IR² / 2(R² + x²)³ᐟ².

questions.text: The SI unit of magnetic field is:
questions.answer: Tesla

questions.text: The magnetic field around a current carrying straight conductor is:
questions.answer: Circular

questions.text: State Fleming's right hand rule.
questions.answer: If the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand are mutually perpendicular, then the forefinger indicates magnetic field, thumb indicates motion of conductor and middle finger indicates induced current.

questions.text: State Biot–Savart law.
questions.answer: The magnetic field due to a small current element is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the square of distance from it.

questions.text: Define magnetic permeability.
questions.answer: Magnetic permeability is the measure of ability of a material to support the formation of magnetic field within it.

questions.text: Why are magnetic field lines continuous closed curves?
questions.answer: Because magnetic monopoles do not exist; field lines neither start nor end but form closed loops.

questions.text: Calculate magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from a long straight conductor carrying 10 A current.
questions.answer: B = μ₀I / 2πr = 1×10⁻⁴ T

questions.text: Find magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 10 cm carrying current 5 A.
Derive an expression for magnetic field at the centre of a circular current carrying coil.
questions.answer: Using Biot–Savart law, B = μ₀I / 2r is obtained at the centre of the coil.

questions.text: Explain the working principle of a moving coil galvanometer.
questions.answer: It works on the principle that a current carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque.

chapters.title: Magnetic Materials
chapters.description: Magnetization, magnetic intensity and susceptibility; dia-, para- and ferromagnetic materials; B–H curves, hysteresis and applications.
learningObjectives: Define magnetization and magnetic susceptibility.
Differentiate between dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances with examples.
Interpret hysteresis loop and relate to energy loss.
Explain why soft iron is used for transformer cores while steel for permanent magnets.
Relate microscopic alignment of domains to macroscopic magnetization.

questions.text: Define magnetization of a material.
questions.answer: Magnetization M is the magnetic moment per unit volume of a material: M = μ_total / V.

questions.text: Which of the following is ferromagnetic at room temperature?
questions.answer: Iron

questions.text: What is magnetic susceptibility? How is it related to relative permeability?
questions.answer: Magnetic susceptibility χ is the ratio of magnetization M to magnetic intensity H: χ = M/H. Relative permeability μ_r is related as μ_r = 1 + χ.

questions.text: Give any two properties of diamagnetic materials.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Weakly repelled by magnetic fields. (ii) χ is small and negative. (iii) μ_r is slightly less than 1. (iv) Independent of temperature.

questions.text: Why does a ferromagnetic material lose its ferromagnetic property above Curie temperature?
questions.answer: Above Curie temperature, thermal agitation becomes strong enough to randomize the orientation of magnetic domains, destroying spontaneous magnetization; the material behaves as paramagnetic.

questions.text: Distinguish between soft and hard magnetic materials based on their hysteresis loops and typical uses.
questions.answer: Soft materials: narrow hysteresis loop, small coercivity and remanence, low energy loss per cycle; used in transformer and electromagnet cores. Hard materials: wide hysteresis loop, large coercivity and remanence, high energy loss but retain magnetization; used for permanent magnets, recording media.

questions.text: A paramagnetic material has susceptibility 2×10⁻³. Find its relative permeability.
Explain the origin of permanent magnetism in ferromagnetic materials in terms of domains.
questions.answer: Ferromagnetic materials consist of small regions called magnetic domains, in each of which atomic magnetic moments are strongly aligned due to exchange interaction. In an unmagnetized specimen, domains are randomly oriented, resulting in zero net magnetization. When an external field is applied, domains aligned with the field grow at the expense of others, giving large net magnetization that can persist even after the field is removed.

questions.text: Why are transformer cores laminated?
questions.answer: They are laminated to reduce eddy currents and thereby decrease energy loss and heating in the core.

questions.text: Draw a typical hysteresis loop for a ferromagnetic material and explain the terms retentivity and coercivity.
questions.answer: On a B–H graph, the loop shows how B changes as H is cycled. Retentivity (remanence) is the value of B remaining when H is reduced to zero after saturation. Coercivity is the value of reverse H required to bring B to zero from its remanent value. Larger retentivity means a stronger permanent magnet; larger coercivity indicates greater resistance to demagnetization.

questions.text: The magnetic susceptibility is given by
questions.answer: M/H

questions.text: The relation between relative permeability (μr) and magnetic susceptibility (χ) is
questions.answer: μr = χ + 1

questions.text: If an electron of charge −e and mass m revolves in an orbit, the angular momentum is
questions.answer: 2m/e

questions.text: The gyromagnetic ratio of an electron is given by
questions.answer: e/2m

Magnetization is defined as

questions.text: SI unit of magnetization is
questions.answer: A/m

questions.text: Give gyromagnetic ratio.
questions.answer: Gyromagnetic ratio is the ratio of magnetic moment to angular momentum of an electron.

questions.text: What is Bohr magneton?
questions.answer: Bohr magneton is the unit of magnetic moment of an electron.

questions.answer: Magnetization is the ratio of magnetic moment to the volume of material.

questions.text: What does the ratio M/H indicate?

questions.text: What is magnetic susceptibility?
questions.answer: Magnetic susceptibility is the ratio of magnetization to magnetic field intensity.

questions.text: State SI unit of magnetic field intensity.

questions.text: Is magnetization a vector quantity?
questions.answer: Yes, magnetization is a vector quantity.

questions.text: Show that orbital magnetic moment of electron is proportional to its angular momentum.
questions.answer: Orbital magnetic moment μ = (e/2m)L, hence proportional to angular momentum.

questions.text: Derive expression for Bohr magneton.

questions.text: Find magnetization of a magnet given mass and density.
questions.answer: M = magnetic moment / volume.
